Finite-Scenario Skew-ttt Regime Models for Trading, Risk-Neutralization, and Derivative Pricing

Gene Boo
Version 2.0, 8 August 2024

Scope and caution. This study develops a finite-scenario modelling framework for research, model development, and controlled pricing experiments. It is not investment advice, a claim of unique arbitrage-free completion of an incomplete market, or a substitute for independent model validation. The central construction deliberately treats the empirical finite-support distribution as the operative model. It must not be represented as a consistent estimator of a nonexistent population MGF for an unbounded Student-ttt or skew-ttt law.

Abstract

This revised study (v2) treats the finite scenario law, rather than the empirical MGF, as the primitive pricing object (originally formulated that way in v1 of this document). The empirical MGF is an exact transform of that governed finite-support law and does not repair the nonexistent population MGF of an unbounded Student-ttt or skew-ttt distribution.

This study develops a unified architecture in which physical returns are modelled by a Markov-switching mixture of standardized skewed Student-ttt distributions, while derivative pricing is performed using finite empirical scenario laws and their exact empirical moment-generating functions. The skew parameter nests the symmetric Student-ttt model, and large degrees of freedom approach the Gaussian limit. However, an unbounded Student-ttt or skew-ttt log-return law has no finite moment-generating function at any nonzero real argument. In particular, setting the degrees of freedom to 303030 does not make E[eX]E[e^X]E[eX] finite.

The proposed resolution is not to claim that the population MGF exists. Instead, the physical model is discretized into a finite probability law. Its empirical MGF is finite by construction and is the exact MGF of that discrete model. Risk-neutral probabilities can then be obtained by empirical Esscher tilting, minimum-relative-entropy projection, or option-constrained entropy calibration. Regime transitions and emissions are jointly constrained so that the discounted underlying is a martingale under the selected pricing measure.

The framework supports direct finite-sum valuation, deterministic convolution, Monte Carlo, Fourier quadrature, Carr-Madan FFT, COS-type methods, and dynamic programming. The study derives the relevant transforms, identifies feasibility and non-uniqueness conditions, distinguishes a log-return Esscher tilt from an entropy projection constrained on gross returns, and specifies tail-completion, numerical-stability, no-arbitrage, convergence, and model-risk controls. It also proposes trading signals based on physical probabilities and relative-value signals based on differences between physical and risk-neutral distributions.

1. Executive conclusions

  1. A mixed skew-ttt regime model is a coherent physical return model:

    Xt+1=μSt+1P+σSt+1PZt+1,Zt+1∣St+1=k∼SkewT⁡∗(νkP,λkP). X_{t+1}=\mu_{S_{t+1}}^P+\sigma_{S_{t+1}}^P Z_{t+1}, \qquad Z_{t+1}\mid S_{t+1}=k\sim \operatorname{SkewT}^{*}(\nu_k^P,\lambda_k^P). Xt+1​=μSt+1​P​+σSt+1​P​Zt+1​,Zt+1​∣St+1​=k∼SkewT∗(νkP​,λkP​).

  2. In a standardized Hansen-style parameterization, λk=0\lambda_k=0λk​=0 returns the symmetric Student-ttt. As νk→∞\nu_k\to\inftyνk​→∞, the symmetric Student-ttt converges in distribution to a Gaussian. A t30t_{30}t30​ law is close to Gaussian in its central body but still has polynomial tails and no nontrivial MGF [1, 2].

  3. For any finite ν\nuν, a genuine unbounded Student-ttt log return satisfies

    E[euX]=∞ E[e^{uX}]=\infty E[euX]=∞

    for every real u≠0u\ne 0u=0. The same problem remains for common skew-ttt constructions with polynomial tails on both sides. Therefore, a raw skew-ttt log-price model cannot directly satisfy the stock martingale condition through a population MGF.

  4. Given finite scenario nodes xix_ixi​ and positive probabilities pip_ipi​, the empirical law

    Fundefined(dx)=∑i=1Npi δxi(dx) \widehat F(dx)=\sum_{i=1}^N p_i\,\delta_{x_i}(dx) F(dx)=i=1∑N​pi​δxi​​(dx)

    has the exact empirical MGF

    Mundefined(u)=∑i=1Npieuxi, \widehat M(u)=\sum_{i=1}^N p_i e^{ux_i}, M(u)=i=1∑N​pi​euxi​,

    which is finite for all finite real or complex uuu.

  5. This finiteness is a property of the chosen finite-support model. It is not evidence that the empirical MGF converges to a finite population MGF as N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞ under an unbounded Student-ttt data-generating law.

  6. An empirical Esscher tilt is valid on the finite scenario space:

    qi(θ)=pieθxi∑jpjeθxj. q_i(\theta)=\frac{p_i e^{\theta x_i}}{\sum_j p_j e^{\theta x_j}}. qi​(θ)=∑j​pj​eθxj​pi​eθxi​​.

    Under this tilt,

    κundefinedQ(u;θ)=κundefinedP(u+θ)−κundefinedP(θ). \widehat\kappa_Q(u;\theta) =\widehat\kappa_P(u+\theta)-\widehat\kappa_P(\theta). κQ​(u;θ)=κP​(u+θ)−κP​(θ).

  7. A minimum-relative-entropy projection subject directly to the tradable gross-return constraint is generally not the same as a log-return Esscher tilt. If the constraint is EQ[eX]=F/S0E_Q[e^X]=F/S_0EQ​[eX]=F/S0​, the entropy solution has the form

    qi(β)=piexp⁡ ⁣(βexi)∑jpjexp⁡ ⁣(βexj), q_i(\beta) =\frac{p_i\exp\!\left(\beta e^{x_i}\right)} {\sum_j p_j\exp\!\left(\beta e^{x_j}\right)}, qi​(β)=∑j​pj​exp(βexj​)pi​exp(βexi​)​,

    where the sign of β\betaβ depends only on the Lagrange-multiplier convention. More generally, constraints on payoff features gm(x)g_m(x)gm​(x) produce an exponential family in those features.

  8. In a regime-switching model, no-arbitrage constrains the combination of risk-neutral transition probabilities and regime emission laws. It does not generally determine them uniquely. Option prices or an explicit selection principle are required to identify the remaining risk premia [3, 4].

  9. A production framework should use the empirical transform as a computational device, while explicitly governing support, tail completion, maturity consistency, weight concentration, and option-surface arbitrage.

2. Mathematical preliminaries

2.1 Prices, returns, and measures

Let StS_tSt​ be the ex-dividend spot price. Over one model step of length Δ\DeltaΔ, define the log return

Xt+Δ=log⁡(St+ΔSt). X_{t+\Delta}=\log\left(\frac{S_{t+\Delta}}{S_t}\right). Xt+Δ​=log(St​St+Δ​​).

Let PPP denote the physical measure used for forecasting and trading analysis, and let QQQ denote a selected equivalent martingale measure used for pricing. With deterministic short rate rtr_trt​ and dividend yield qtq_tqt​, define the one-step carry

ct=∫tt+Δ(ru−qu) du. c_t=\int_t^{t+\Delta}(r_u-q_u)\,du. ct​=∫tt+Δ​(ru​−qu​)du.

The one-step martingale restriction is

EQ[eXt+Δ∣Ft]=ect. E_Q\left[e^{X_{t+\Delta}}\mid\mathcal F_t\right]=e^{c_t}. EQ​[eXt+Δ​∣Ft​]=ect​.

Equivalently,

EQ[St+Δ∣Ft]=Stect. E_Q[S_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_t]=S_t e^{c_t}. EQ​[St+Δ​∣Ft​]=St​ect​.

This condition concerns the exponential of the log return, not merely the mean of the log return.

2.2 MGF, CGF, and characteristic function

For a random variable XXX, the MGF is

MX(u)=E[euX], M_X(u)=E[e^{uX}], MX​(u)=E[euX],

where the expectation is finite. The cumulant-generating function is

κX(u)=log⁡MX(u). \kappa_X(u)=\log M_X(u). κX​(u)=logMX​(u).

The characteristic function is

ϕX(v)=E[eivX],v∈R. \phi_X(v)=E[e^{ivX}], \qquad v\in\mathbb R. ϕX​(v)=E[eivX],v∈R.

The characteristic function always exists because ∣eivX∣=1|e^{ivX}|=1∣eivX∣=1. The MGF need not exist because euXe^{uX}euX is unbounded for real u≠0u\ne0u=0.

2.3 Why Student-ttt has no nontrivial MGF

For a Student-ttt variable with ν\nuν degrees of freedom, the density has polynomial tails:

fX(x)≍C∣x∣−(ν+1) f_X(x)\asymp C|x|^{-(\nu+1)} fX​(x)≍C∣x∣−(ν+1)

as ∣x∣→∞|x|\to\infty∣x∣→∞. For any u>0u>0u>0, the positive tail of

∫−∞∞euxfX(x) dx \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{ux}f_X(x)\,dx ∫−∞∞​euxfX​(x)dx

behaves like euxx−(ν+1)e^{ux}x^{-(\nu+1)}euxx−(ν+1) and diverges. For any u<0u<0u<0, the negative tail diverges. Hence

MX(u)=∞,u≠0. M_X(u)=\infty,\qquad u\ne0. MX​(u)=∞,u=0.

The existence of many ordinary moments when ν\nuν is large does not imply existence of the MGF. A Student-ttt with ν=30\nu=30ν=30 has finite moments only up to orders below 303030, while an MGF finite in a neighborhood of zero would imply moments of all orders.

3. Physical mixed skew-ttt regime model

3.1 Hidden regime process

Let

St∈{1,…,K} S_t\in\{1,\ldots,K\} St​∈{1,…,K}

be a latent regime following a first-order Markov chain:

pijP=P(St+1=j∣St=i). p_{ij}^P=P(S_{t+1}=j\mid S_t=i). pijP​=P(St+1​=j∣St​=i).

The matrix PP=(pijP)P^P=(p_{ij}^P)PP=(pijP​) is row stochastic:

pijP≥0,∑j=1KpijP=1. p_{ij}^P\ge0, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^Kp_{ij}^P=1. pijP​≥0,j=1∑K​pijP​=1.

Hamilton’s filtering framework provides a standard basis for estimating latent discrete-state models and forecasting regime probabilities [5].

3.2 Standardized skew-ttt emissions

Use

Xt+1=μSt+1P+σSt+1PZt+1, X_{t+1}=\mu_{S_{t+1}}^P+\sigma_{S_{t+1}}^P Z_{t+1}, Xt+1​=μSt+1​P​+σSt+1​P​Zt+1​,

where

Zt+1∣St+1=k∼SkewT⁡∗(νkP,λkP), Z_{t+1}\mid S_{t+1}=k \sim\operatorname{SkewT}^{*}(\nu_k^P,\lambda_k^P), Zt+1​∣St+1​=k∼SkewT∗(νkP​,λkP​),

and the standardized innovation satisfies

EP[Zt+1∣St+1=k]=0,Var⁡P(Zt+1∣St+1=k)=1. E_P[Z_{t+1}\mid S_{t+1}=k]=0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}_P(Z_{t+1}\mid S_{t+1}=k)=1. EP​[Zt+1​∣St+1​=k]=0,VarP​(Zt+1​∣St+1​=k)=1.

Accordingly,

EP[Xt+1∣St+1=k]=μkP, E_P[X_{t+1}\mid S_{t+1}=k]=\mu_k^P, EP​[Xt+1​∣St+1​=k]=μkP​,

and

Var⁡P(Xt+1∣St+1=k)=(σkP)2. \operatorname{Var}_P(X_{t+1}\mid S_{t+1}=k)=(\sigma_k^P)^2. VarP​(Xt+1​∣St+1​=k)=(σkP​)2.

This standardization is operationally important because in several skew-ttt parameterizations the raw location parameter is not the mean and the raw scale parameter is not the standard deviation.

3.3 Nesting structure

For the Hansen skewed Student density [1]:

λk=0⟹SkewT⁡∗(νk,λk)=tνk∗. \lambda_k=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{SkewT}^{*}(\nu_k,\lambda_k) = t_{\nu_k}^{*}. λk​=0⟹SkewT∗(νk​,λk​)=tνk​∗​.

Then

νk→∞⟹tνk∗⇒N(0,1). \nu_k\to\infty \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t_{\nu_k}^{*}\Rightarrow N(0,1). νk​→∞⟹tνk​∗​⇒N(0,1).

Thus the parameter space contains a symmetric Student-ttt submodel and approaches a Gaussian limit.

For the symmetric tνt_\nutν​ with ν>4\nu>4ν>4, excess kurtosis is

γ2=6ν−4. \gamma_2=\frac{6}{\nu-4}. γ2​=ν−46​.

At ν=30\nu=30ν=30,

γ2=626≈0.230769. \gamma_2=\frac{6}{26}\approx0.230769. γ2​=266​≈0.230769.

Therefore t30t_{30}t30​ is visibly close to normal in the body but is not exactly Gaussian and remains fundamentally different in the far tails.

3.4 Suggested parsimonious starting model

A three-state model may be initialized as follows:

  • Quiet state: λ1=0\lambda_1=0λ1​=0, ν1=30\nu_1=30ν1​=30.
  • Stress state: λ2<0\lambda_2<0λ2​<0, 4<ν2<124<\nu_2<124<ν2​<12.
  • Recovery or squeeze state: λ3>0\lambda_3>0λ3​>0, 4<ν3<154<\nu_3<154<ν3​<15.

A stable first specification can constrain

ν2=ν3=νtail \nu_2=\nu_3=\nu_{\text{tail}} ν2​=ν3​=νtail​

and optionally

λ3=−λ2. \lambda_3=-\lambda_2. λ3​=−λ2​.

These restrictions can later be relaxed only if the resulting parameters remain identifiable and improve out-of-sample density and tail forecasts.

3.5 Physical filtering and forecasting

Let

αt,kP=P(St=k∣Ft) \alpha_{t,k}^P=P(S_t=k\mid\mathcal F_t) αt,kP​=P(St​=k∣Ft​)

be the filtered state probabilities. Prediction gives

αt+1∣t,jP=∑i=1Kαt,iPpijP. \alpha_{t+1\mid t,j}^P =\sum_{i=1}^K\alpha_{t,i}^Pp_{ij}^P. αt+1∣t,jP​=i=1∑K​αt,iP​pijP​.

After observing Xt+1=xX_{t+1}=xXt+1​=x, update by Bayes’ rule:

αt+1,jP=αt+1∣t,jPfjP(x)∑ℓ=1Kαt+1∣t,ℓPfℓP(x). \alpha_{t+1,j}^P =\frac{ \alpha_{t+1\mid t,j}^P f_j^P(x) }{ \sum_{\ell=1}^K\alpha_{t+1\mid t,\ell}^P f_\ell^P(x) }. αt+1,jP​=∑ℓ=1K​αt+1∣t,ℓP​fℓP​(x)αt+1∣t,jP​fjP​(x)​.

For live trading and historical backtesting, filtered probabilities must use only information available at the relevant time. Smoothed probabilities condition on future observations and therefore must not be used as if they were contemporaneously observable signals.

4. Finite empirical scenario law

4.1 Definition

For regime kkk, define scenario nodes and physical weights

{(xk,i,pk,iP)}i=1Nk, \{(x_{k,i},p_{k,i}^P)\}_{i=1}^{N_k}, {(xk,i​,pk,iP​)}i=1Nk​​,

with

pk,iP>0,∑i=1Nkpk,iP=1. p_{k,i}^P>0, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{N_k}p_{k,i}^P=1. pk,iP​>0,i=1∑Nk​​pk,iP​=1.

The empirical regime law is

FundefinedkP(dx)=∑i=1Nkpk,iPδxk,i(dx). \widehat F_k^P(dx) =\sum_{i=1}^{N_k}p_{k,i}^P\delta_{x_{k,i}}(dx). FkP​(dx)=i=1∑Nk​​pk,iP​δxk,i​​(dx).

The strict positivity requirement is convenient if equivalence of PPP and QQQ on the finite support is desired. If piP=0p_i^P=0piP​=0, an absolutely continuous change of measure cannot assign that node positive QQQ-probability.

4.2 Construction alternatives

Weighted historical law

If γt,k\gamma_{t,k}γt,k​ is a regime responsibility, define

pk,tP=γt,k∑sγs,k. p_{k,t}^P =\frac{\gamma_{t,k}}{\sum_s\gamma_{s,k}}. pk,tP​=∑s​γs,k​γt,k​​.

This uses observed returns but may undersample rare tails.

Deterministic quantile grid

Choose probabilities uiu_iui​ and define

xk,i=Fk−1(ui). x_{k,i}=F_k^{-1}(u_i). xk,i​=Fk−1​(ui​).

For an equal-probability midpoint grid,

ui=i−12Nk,pk,iP=1Nk. u_i=\frac{i-\tfrac12}{N_k}, \qquad p_{k,i}^P=\frac1{N_k}. ui​=Nk​i−21​​,pk,iP​=Nk​1​.

A tail-enriched grid uses nonuniform cells and assigns each node the exact probability mass of its cell.

Hybrid body and stress nodes

Combine historical observations, fitted skew-ttt quantiles, and explicit stress nodes. The probabilities must then be normalized and documented. Stress-node probabilities are model assumptions, not empirical facts.

4.4 Stable numerical evaluation

Define

ai(u)=log⁡pi+uxi,m(u)=max⁡iai(u). a_i(u)=\log p_i+ux_i, \qquad m(u)=\max_i a_i(u). ai​(u)=logpi​+uxi​,m(u)=imax​ai​(u).

Then

κundefined(u)=m(u)+log⁡∑iexp⁡(ai(u)−m(u)). \widehat\kappa(u) =m(u)+\log\sum_i\exp(a_i(u)-m(u)). κ(u)=m(u)+logi∑​exp(ai​(u)−m(u)).

This log-sum-exp form should be mandatory. Direct exponentiation can overflow or underflow and may silently corrupt the risk-neutral calibration.

5. What empirical-MGF finiteness does and does not mean

5.1 Exact statement

For fixed finite nodes and weights, MundefinedN(u)\widehat M_N(u)MN​(u) is the exact MGF of the empirical discrete law. Every exponential moment exists.

5.2 Incorrect statement to avoid

It is incorrect to claim that

MundefinedN(u)→MX(u)<∞ \widehat M_N(u)\to M_X(u)<\infty MN​(u)→MX​(u)<∞

for samples drawn from an unbounded Student-ttt population and real u≠0u\ne0u=0.

5.3 Extreme-node instability

Let

X(N)=max⁡1≤i≤NXi. X_{(N)}=\max_{1\le i\le N}X_i. X(N)​=1≤i≤Nmax​Xi​.

For equal weights,

MundefinedN(1)=1N∑i=1NeXi≥eX(N)N. \widehat M_N(1) =\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Ne^{X_i} \ge\frac{e^{X_{(N)}}}{N}. MN​(1)=N1​i=1∑N​eXi​≥NeX(N)​​.

As new heavy-tailed observations increase the maximum, the empirical exponential moment can jump discontinuously in economic terms. Apparent stability over a finite historical window is not convergence evidence.

5.4 Correct interpretation

The empirical MGF defines a finite-horizon, finite-support model. Its validity depends on:

  • the support policy;
  • tail-node design;
  • scenario probabilities;
  • calibration instruments;
  • maturity horizon;
  • sensitivity to extreme nodes.

6. Empirical risk-neutralization

6.1 Empirical log-return Esscher tilt

Define

qiE(θ)=piPeθxi∑jpjPeθxj. q_i^{E}(\theta) =\frac{p_i^P e^{\theta x_i}} {\sum_jp_j^P e^{\theta x_j}}. qiE​(θ)=∑j​pjP​eθxj​piP​eθxi​​.

Then

MundefinedQE(u;θ)=∑iqiE(θ)euxi=MundefinedP(u+θ)MundefinedP(θ), \widehat M_Q^E(u;\theta) =\sum_iq_i^E(\theta)e^{ux_i} =\frac{\widehat M_P(u+\theta)}{\widehat M_P(\theta)}, MQE​(u;θ)=i∑​qiE​(θ)euxi​=MP​(θ)MP​(u+θ)​,

and

κundefinedQE(u;θ)=κundefinedP(u+θ)−κundefinedP(θ). \widehat\kappa_Q^E(u;\theta) =\widehat\kappa_P(u+\theta)-\widehat\kappa_P(\theta). κQE​(u;θ)=κP​(u+θ)−κP​(θ).

This is the exact Esscher identity on the empirical support. Esscher-based option pricing selects a martingale measure by exponential tilting when the relevant transform exists [3].

6.2 One-regime martingale equation

For one period with carry ccc, require

MundefinedQE(1;θ)=ec. \widehat M_Q^E(1;\theta)=e^c. MQE​(1;θ)=ec.

Equivalently,

κundefinedP(θ+1)−κundefinedP(θ)=c. \boxed{ \widehat\kappa_P(\theta+1)-\widehat\kappa_P(\theta)=c. } κP​(θ+1)−κP​(θ)=c.​

Define

g(θ)=κundefinedP(θ+1)−κundefinedP(θ). g(\theta)=\widehat\kappa_P(\theta+1)-\widehat\kappa_P(\theta). g(θ)=κP​(θ+1)−κP​(θ).

The derivative is

g′(θ)=κundefinedP′(θ+1)−κundefinedP′(θ)≥0 g'(\theta) =\widehat\kappa_P'(\theta+1)-\widehat\kappa_P'(\theta)\ge0 g′(θ)=κP′​(θ+1)−κP′​(θ)≥0

because κundefinedP′\widehat\kappa_P'κP′​ is nondecreasing. With a nondegenerate support, strict monotonicity normally holds.

As θ→−∞\theta\to-\inftyθ→−∞, the tilted mass concentrates on xmin⁡x_{\min}xmin​, giving

g(θ)→xmin⁡. g(\theta)\to x_{\min}. g(θ)→xmin​.

As θ→+∞\theta\to+\inftyθ→+∞,

g(θ)→xmax⁡. g(\theta)\to x_{\max}. g(θ)→xmax​.

Therefore a finite solution exists when

xmin⁡<c<xmax⁡. \boxed{x_{\min}<c<x_{\max}.} xmin​<c<xmax​.​

At the boundary, the solution requires a limiting degenerate measure concentrated at an extreme node, not a finite θ\thetaθ. For a tradable gross return, this condition is equivalently

exmin⁡<ec<exmax⁡. e^{x_{\min}}<e^c<e^{x_{\max}}. exmin​<ec<exmax​.

6.3 Minimum-relative-entropy projection

Instead of restricting QQQ to a log-return Esscher family, solve

min⁡q∈ΔNDKL(q∥p)=min⁡q∑iqilog⁡(qipi) \min_{q\in\Delta_N} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p) =\min_q\sum_iq_i\log\left(\frac{q_i}{p_i}\right) q∈ΔN​min​DKL​(q∥p)=qmin​i∑​qi​log(pi​qi​​)

subject to

∑iqi=1,∑iqigm(xi)=bm,m=1,…,M. \sum_iq_i=1, \qquad \sum_iq_i g_m(x_i)=b_m, \quad m=1,\ldots,M. i∑​qi​=1,i∑​qi​gm​(xi​)=bm​,m=1,…,M.

The solution has exponential-family form

qi(β)=piexp⁡(∑m=1Mβmgm(xi))∑jpjexp⁡(∑m=1Mβmgm(xj)). \boxed{ q_i(\boldsymbol\beta) =\frac{p_i\exp\left(\sum_{m=1}^M\beta_m g_m(x_i)\right)} {\sum_jp_j\exp\left(\sum_{m=1}^M\beta_m g_m(x_j)\right)}. } qi​(β)=∑j​pj​exp(∑m=1M​βm​gm​(xj​))pi​exp(∑m=1M​βm​gm​(xi​))​.​

This follows from the Lagrangian first-order conditions. Maximum-entropy and relative-entropy projections under expectation constraints generate exponential-family solutions [6, 7].

If the sole pricing constraint is the forward condition,

g1(x)=ex,b1=ec, g_1(x)=e^x, \qquad b_1=e^c, g1​(x)=ex,b1​=ec,

then

qi(β)=piexp⁡(βexi)∑jpjexp⁡(βexj). \boxed{ q_i(\beta) =\frac{p_i\exp(\beta e^{x_i})} {\sum_jp_j\exp(\beta e^{x_j})}. } qi​(β)=∑j​pj​exp(βexj​)pi​exp(βexi​)​.​

This is generally different from

qiE(θ)∝pieθxi. q_i^E(\theta)\propto p_ie^{\theta x_i}. qiE​(θ)∝pi​eθxi​.

The two coincide only in special or approximate circumstances. Confusing these two tilts is a material mathematical error.

6.4 Feasibility of entropy calibration

The constraint vector b=(b1,…,bM)\mathbf b=(b_1,\ldots,b_M)b=(b1​,…,bM​) must lie in the convex hull of the feature vectors

g(xi)=(g1(xi),…,gM(xi)). \mathbf g(x_i) =(g_1(x_i),\ldots,g_M(x_i)). g(xi​)=(g1​(xi​),…,gM​(xi​)).

For the one-dimensional forward constraint, feasibility requires

min⁡iexi≤ec≤max⁡iexi. \min_i e^{x_i} \le e^c\le \max_i e^{x_i}. imin​exi​≤ec≤imax​exi​.

Strict interior feasibility yields strictly positive calibrated probabilities. Boundary feasibility generally produces concentration on boundary nodes.

6.5 Option-constrained entropy calibration

At maturity TTT, let terminal node iii imply ST,iS_{T,i}ST,i​ and discounted payoff

Gm,i=D(0,T)Πm(ST,i). G_{m,i}=D(0,T)\Pi_m(S_{T,i}). Gm,i​=D(0,T)Πm​(ST,i​).

A robust calibration is

min⁡qDKL(q∥p)+λRR(q) \min_q D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p)+\lambda_R\mathcal R(q) qmin​DKL​(q∥p)+λR​R(q)

subject to

qi≥0,∑iqi=1, q_i\ge0, \qquad \sum_iq_i=1, qi​≥0,i∑​qi​=1,

∑iqiST,i=F0,T, \sum_iq_iS_{T,i}=F_{0,T}, i∑​qi​ST,i​=F0,T​,

and bid-ask constraints

Vmbid≤∑iqiGm,i≤Vmask. V_m^{\mathrm{bid}} \le \sum_iq_iG_{m,i} \le V_m^{\mathrm{ask}}. Vmbid​≤i∑​qi​Gm,i​≤Vmask​.

Exact equality to option mids should be used only when quotes are reliable and jointly arbitrage-consistent. Option prices reveal state-price information through strike derivatives, forming the basis of risk-neutral density recovery [8].

6.6 Incompleteness and selection of QQQ

A martingale condition supplies restrictions, not a unique risk-neutral measure, when the model contains unhedgeable regime and jump risks. Empirical Esscher tilting, minimum entropy, and direct option calibration are alternative measure-selection rules. They should be compared rather than treated as universally equivalent [3, 4].

7. Regime-switching risk-neutral dynamics

7.1 Risk-neutral transitions

Let

PQ=(pijQ) P^Q=(p_{ij}^Q) PQ=(pijQ​)

be the risk-neutral transition matrix. In general,

PQ≠PP. P^Q\ne P^P. PQ=PP.

The difference represents regime-transition risk premia and must be inferred from option prices, constrained economically, or selected through a pricing-kernel principle.

7.2 Emissions attached to the arriving state

Assume the one-step return distribution depends on St+1=jS_{t+1}=jSt+1​=j. Let

mjQ(u)=EQ[euXt+1∣St+1=j] m_j^Q(u)=E_Q[e^{uX_{t+1}}\mid S_{t+1}=j] mjQ​(u)=EQ​[euXt+1​∣St+1​=j]

be the regime empirical MGF. Define

DQ(u)=diag⁡(m1Q(u),…,mKQ(u)). D^Q(u)=\operatorname{diag}(m_1^Q(u),\ldots,m_K^Q(u)). DQ(u)=diag(m1Q​(u),…,mKQ​(u)).

With current state-probability column vector αtQ\boldsymbol\alpha_t^QαtQ​, the hhh-step MGF is

Mt,hQ(u)=(αtQ)⊤[PQDQ(u)]h1. \boxed{ M_{t,h}^Q(u) =(\boldsymbol\alpha_t^Q)^\top \left[P^QD^Q(u)\right]^h\mathbf1. } Mt,hQ​(u)=(αtQ​)⊤[PQDQ(u)]h1.​

This ordering is correct for emissions associated with the arriving state. If emissions are associated with the departing state, the ordering changes to DQ(u)PQD^Q(u)P^QDQ(u)PQ. The convention must be fixed consistently throughout estimation, simulation, and pricing.

The characteristic function is

ϕt,hQ(v)=Mt,hQ(iv). \phi_{t,h}^Q(v)=M_{t,h}^Q(iv). ϕt,hQ​(v)=Mt,hQ​(iv).

7.3 Conditional martingale restriction by current state

For each current state iii,

EQ[eXt+1∣St=i]=∑j=1KpijQmjQ(1). E_Q[e^{X_{t+1}}\mid S_t=i] =\sum_{j=1}^Kp_{ij}^Qm_j^Q(1). EQ​[eXt+1​∣St​=i]=j=1∑K​pijQ​mjQ​(1).

The one-step stock martingale condition requires

∑j=1KpijQmjQ(1)=ect,i=1,…,K. \boxed{ \sum_{j=1}^Kp_{ij}^Qm_j^Q(1)=e^{c_t}, \qquad i=1,\ldots,K. } j=1∑K​pijQ​mjQ​(1)=ect​,i=1,…,K.​

In matrix form,

PQmQ(1)=ect1. \boxed{ P^Q\mathbf m^Q(1)=e^{c_t}\mathbf1. } PQmQ(1)=ect​1.​

A sufficient but stronger restriction is

mjQ(1)=ect m_j^Q(1)=e^{c_t} mjQ​(1)=ect​

for every regime jjj. This makes the martingale condition hold for any transition matrix, but it suppresses possible compensation between transition risk and state-conditional expected gross returns. It is a modelling choice, not a necessity.

7.4 Multi-step martingale consistency

If the one-step condition holds conditionally for every current state and carry is deterministic, iterated expectations imply

EQ[eXt,h∣Ft]=e∑ℓ=0h−1ct+ℓ, E_Q[e^{X_{t,h}}\mid\mathcal F_t] =e^{\sum_{\ell=0}^{h-1}c_{t+\ell}}, EQ​[eXt,h​∣Ft​]=e∑ℓ=0h−1​ct+ℓ​,

where

Xt,h=∑ℓ=1hXt+ℓ. X_{t,h}=\sum_{\ell=1}^hX_{t+\ell}. Xt,h​=ℓ=1∑h​Xt+ℓ​.

If rates, dividends, or transition matrices are state dependent, the discounting and state process must be included jointly. A scalar deterministic correction is then generally insufficient.

8. Trading models under the physical measure

8.1 Horizon distribution

The physical hhh-step characteristic function can be propagated as

ϕt,hP(v)=(αtP)⊤[PPDP(iv)]h1. \phi_{t,h}^P(v) =(\boldsymbol\alpha_t^P)^\top \left[P^PD^P(iv)\right]^h\mathbf1. ϕt,hP​(v)=(αtP​)⊤[PPDP(iv)]h1.

Alternatively, the full distribution can be generated by deterministic convolution or Monte Carlo.

8.2 Trading quantities

Expected log return:

μt,hP=EP[Xt,h∣Ft]. \mu_{t,h}^P=E_P[X_{t,h}\mid\mathcal F_t]. μt,hP​=EP​[Xt,h​∣Ft​].

Probability of a positive return:

pt,h+=PP(Xt,h>0∣Ft). p_{t,h}^{+}=P_P(X_{t,h}>0\mid\mathcal F_t). pt,h+​=PP​(Xt,h​>0∣Ft​).

pt,hG=PP(Xt,h>G∣Ft). p_{t,h}^{G}=P_P(X_{t,h}>G\mid\mathcal F_t). pt,hG​=PP​(Xt,h​>G∣Ft​).

pt,hL=PP(Xt,h<−L∣Ft). p_{t,h}^{L}=P_P(X_{t,h}<-L\mid\mathcal F_t). pt,hL​=PP​(Xt,h​<−L∣Ft​).

VaR⁡αP=inf⁡{ℓ:PP(Lt,h≤ℓ)≥α}. \operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}^P =\inf\{\ell:P_P(L_{t,h}\le\ell)\ge\alpha\}. VaRαP​=inf{ℓ:PP​(Lt,h​≤ℓ)≥α}.

Expected Shortfall:

ES⁡αP=EP[Lt,h∣Lt,h≥VaR⁡αP] \operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}^P =E_P[L_{t,h}\mid L_{t,h}\ge\operatorname{VaR}_{\alpha}^P] ESαP​=EP​[Lt,h​∣Lt,h​≥VaRαP​]

for continuous losses, with the usual quantile-integral definition preferred in discrete laws to handle atoms correctly:

ES⁡αP=11−α∫α1VaR⁡uP du. \operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}^P =\frac{1}{1-\alpha} \int_{\alpha}^{1}\operatorname{VaR}_{u}^P\,du. ESαP​=1−α1​∫α1​VaRuP​du.

8.3 Trade-specific expected utility or payoff

For a proposed trade payoff Πtrade(Xt,h)\Pi_{\text{trade}}(X_{t,h})Πtrade​(Xt,h​),

Edge⁡t,h=EP[Πtrade(Xt,h)∣Ft]−costs. \operatorname{Edge}_{t,h} =E_P[\Pi_{\text{trade}}(X_{t,h})\mid\mathcal F_t]-\text{costs}. Edget,h​=EP​[Πtrade​(Xt,h​)∣Ft​]−costs.

A risk-adjusted score may be

Score⁡t,h=EP[Πtrade]−costsES⁡αP(Ltrade). \operatorname{Score}_{t,h} =\frac{E_P[\Pi_{\text{trade}}]-\text{costs}} {\operatorname{ES}_{\alpha}^P(L_{\text{trade}})}. Scoret,h​=ESαP​(Ltrade​)EP​[Πtrade​]−costs​.

This is a design choice rather than a theorem. Position sizing must also include turnover, liquidity, limits, drawdown, and model uncertainty.

8.4 Physical versus risk-neutral divergence

For a region AAA,

Δpt,h(A)=PP(Xt,h∈A∣Ft)−PQ(Xt,h∈A∣Ft). \Delta p_{t,h}(A) =P_P(X_{t,h}\in A\mid\mathcal F_t) -P_Q(X_{t,h}\in A\mid\mathcal F_t). Δpt,h​(A)=PP​(Xt,h​∈A∣Ft​)−PQ​(Xt,h​∈A∣Ft​).

This can support option relative-value analysis, but the difference includes risk premia, market frictions, and model error. It is not automatically an arbitrage signal.

9. Derivative pricing engines

9.1 Direct finite-sum valuation

For a one-period payoff Π(ST)\Pi(S_T)Π(ST​) under terminal nodes xix_ixi​,

V0=D(0,T)∑iqiQΠ(S0exi). \boxed{ V_0=D(0,T)\sum_iq_i^Q\Pi(S_0e^{x_i}). } V0​=D(0,T)i∑​qiQ​Π(S0​exi​).​

This is exact under the finite empirical model. It is the primary unit-test benchmark for other engines.

9.2 Deterministic convolution

For independent conditional increments, finite discrete laws can be convolved. In a regime model, propagate a vector of state-conditioned mass functions. After each step:

  1. transition regime probabilities;
  2. convolve with the arriving-state emission law;
  3. project onto a controlled log-price grid if necessary;
  4. preserve total mass and the discounted first moment.

Projection introduces numerical error and must be separated from model error.

9.3 Monte Carlo

For each risk-neutral path:

  1. draw the next state from PQP^QPQ;
  2. draw a scenario node from the corresponding qk,iQq_{k,i}^Qqk,iQ​;
  3. update St+Δ=Stexk,iS_{t+\Delta}=S_te^{x_{k,i}}St+Δ​=St​exk,i​;
  4. continue until maturity;
  5. evaluate and discount the payoff.

The estimator is

Vundefined0MC=D(0,T)1M∑m=1MΠ(m). \widehat V_0^{MC} =D(0,T)\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\Pi^{(m)}. V0MC​=D(0,T)M1​m=1∑M​Π(m).

Its estimated standard error is

SE⁡undefined(Vundefined0MC)=D(0,T)sΠM. \widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat V_0^{MC}) =D(0,T)\frac{s_\Pi}{\sqrt M}. SE(V0MC​)=D(0,T)M​sΠ​​.

Monte Carlo is appropriate for barriers, Asians, cliquets, callable structures, and other path-dependent products. Variance reduction should use controls such as a matched Gaussian model, stratification by state path, antithetics where meaningful, conditional expectation, or quasi-Monte Carlo.

9.4 Fourier transform and FFT

The empirical terminal characteristic function is

ϕTQ(v)=∑iqiQeivxi. \phi_T^Q(v)=\sum_iq_i^Qe^{ivx_i}. ϕTQ​(v)=i∑​qiQ​eivxi​.

For the regime model it is obtained through the matrix recursion above.

Carr-Madan pricing applies exponential damping to a call-price function and evaluates the characteristic function at a complex-shifted argument [9]. For damping parameter α>0\alpha>0α>0, sufficient integrability includes

EQ[STα+1]<∞. E_Q[S_T^{\alpha+1}]<\infty. EQ​[STα+1​]<∞.

In the empirical finite-support model,

EQ[e(α+1)XT]<∞ E_Q[e^{(\alpha+1)X_T}]<\infty EQ​[e(α+1)XT​]<∞

for every finite α\alphaα, but only because the support is finite. The admissible numerical α\alphaα should still be chosen to control overflow, truncation, and oscillation.

The shifted transform can be evaluated directly as

ϕTQ(v−i(α+1))=EQ[eivXTe(α+1)XT]. \phi_T^Q(v-i(\alpha+1)) =E_Q[e^{ivX_T}e^{(\alpha+1)X_T}]. ϕTQ​(v−i(α+1))=EQ​[eivXT​e(α+1)XT​].

FFT is valuable for pricing many strikes simultaneously, while direct Fourier quadrature is often simpler and more accurate for isolated strikes. Carr and Madan show how a known characteristic function can be used for efficient option valuation by FFT [9].

9.5 Quadrature

For a smoothed terminal density fTQ(x)f_T^Q(x)fTQ​(x),

V0=D(0,T)∫−∞∞Π(S0ex)fTQ(x) dx. V_0=D(0,T)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \Pi(S_0e^x)f_T^Q(x)\,dx. V0​=D(0,T)∫−∞∞​Π(S0​ex)fTQ​(x)dx.

For an unsmoothed empirical law, this integral is exactly a finite sum. Quadrature becomes relevant after kernel smoothing, interpolated density construction, or continuous tail completion.

Recommended methods include:

  • adaptive Gauss-Kronrod;
  • domain splitting at payoff kinks;
  • double-exponential quadrature for difficult tails;
  • Gauss-Legendre after a finite-domain map;
  • Gauss-Hermite when a conditional Gaussian representation is used.

9.6 American and path-dependent products

American pricing requires dynamic programming or least-squares Monte Carlo. The state vector should include at least spot and latent-state information. If only filtered regime probabilities are observable, exercise policies should be expressed in terms of (St,αtQ)(S_t,\boldsymbol\alpha_t^Q)(St​,αtQ​) rather than an unobservable true state.

10. Greeks and hedging

10.1 Delta under a fixed terminal empirical law

For a European call,

C0=D(0,T)∑iqiQ(S0exi−K)+. C_0=D(0,T)\sum_iq_i^Q(S_0e^{x_i}-K)^+. C0​=D(0,T)i∑​qiQ​(S0​exi​−K)+.

If the calibrated weights and return nodes are held fixed with respect to S0S_0S0​, then away from node-specific payoff kinks,

Δ=D(0,T)∑iqiQexi1{S0exi>K}. \Delta =D(0,T)\sum_iq_i^Qe^{x_i} \mathbf1_{\{S_0e^{x_i}>K\}}. Δ=D(0,T)i∑​qiQ​exi​1{S0​exi​>K}​.

10.2 Calibration-aware Greeks

In production, qiQq_i^QqiQ​, nodes, forwards, and implied parameters may depend on spot. A full Greek must account for recalibration or specify a sticky rule. The fixed-law derivative above is not automatically the desk hedge.

10.3 Gamma roughness

A purely discrete terminal law produces atoms and therefore non-smooth strike and spot Greeks. Remedies include:

  • kernel smoothing;
  • entropy-smoothed interpolation;
  • local continuous distributions around nodes;
  • option-consistent spline densities;
  • a sufficiently fine convolution grid.

Smoothing must preserve probability, the forward, and nonnegative density.

11. Tail policy

11.1 Why tail policy cannot be omitted

The empirical model cannot generate values outside its support. Deep-out-of-the-money options and long-horizon exponential moments can therefore be dominated by arbitrary endpoint choices.

11.2 Permissible policies

Hard bounded support

Specify

Lk≤Xk≤Uk. L_k\le X_k\le U_k. Lk​≤Xk​≤Uk​.

This is transparent but imposes absolute bounds.

Truncated skew-ttt

For fitted skew-ttt CDF FkF_kFk​, choose

Lk=Fk−1(εk−),Uk=Fk−1(1−εk+). L_k=F_k^{-1}(\varepsilon_k^-), \qquad U_k=F_k^{-1}(1-\varepsilon_k^+). Lk​=Fk−1​(εk−​),Uk​=Fk−1​(1−εk+​).

The truncated density is

fktr(x)=fk(x)1[Lk,Uk](x)Fk(Uk)−Fk(Lk). f_k^{\mathrm{tr}}(x) =\frac{f_k(x)\mathbf1_{[L_k,U_k]}(x)} {F_k(U_k)-F_k(L_k)}. fktr​(x)=Fk​(Uk​)−Fk​(Lk​)fk​(x)1[Lk​,Uk​]​(x)​.

Continuous tail completion

Use an empirical or skew-ttt body and attach integrable left and right tails. This is effectively a new tempered or spliced distribution and must be labelled accordingly.

Option-implied tail nodes

Add nodes beyond historical support and infer their QQQ weights from liquid option prices under regularization. This is the preferred empirical derivative-pricing approach when strikes extend beyond the historical scenario range.

11.3 Boundary sensitivity

Every material output should be recalculated under several support policies. A price that changes substantially when a single remote node is added is tail-policy dominated.

12. Calibration architecture

12.1 Physical calibration

Estimate

ΘP={PP,μkP,σkP,νkP,λkP}k=1K \Theta^P =\{P^P,\mu_k^P,\sigma_k^P,\nu_k^P,\lambda_k^P\}_{k=1}^K ΘP={PP,μkP​,σkP​,νkP​,λkP​}k=1K​

by maximum likelihood, Bayesian inference, or penalized likelihood.

Useful constraints include

σkP>0,νkP>2,−1<λkP<1 \sigma_k^P>0, \qquad \nu_k^P>2, \qquad -1<\lambda_k^P<1 σkP​>0,νkP​>2,−1<λkP​<1

for the Hansen parameterization. If fourth moments are operationally needed, constrain

νkP>4. \nu_k^P>4. νkP​>4.

Use state-ordering restrictions, such as

σ1P<σ2P<⋯<σKP, \sigma_1^P<\sigma_2^P<\cdots<\sigma_K^P, σ1P​<σ2P​<⋯<σKP​,

to reduce label switching.

12.2 Risk-neutral calibration

Risk-neutral parameters may include

PQ,θk,qk,i,TQ, P^Q, \qquad \theta_k, \qquad q_{k,i,T}^Q, PQ,θk​,qk,i,TQ​,

subject to martingale and arbitrage constraints.

A representative objective is

J=∑mwm(Vmmodel−Vmmidmax⁡(sm,smin⁡))2+λKLDKL(Q∥P)+λRR(Q). \mathcal J =\sum_mw_m \left( \frac{V_m^{\mathrm{model}}-V_m^{\mathrm{mid}}} {\max(s_m,s_{\min})} \right)^2 +\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\Vert P) +\lambda_R\mathcal R(Q). J=m∑​wm​(max(sm​,smin​)Vmmodel​−Vmmid​​)2+λKL​DKL​(Q∥P)+λR​R(Q).

The regularizer may penalize:

  • abrupt adjacent-node weight changes;
  • transition matrices far from PPP^PPP;
  • concentrated weights;
  • maturity-to-maturity instability;
  • excessive tail-node mass.

12.3 Exact constraints versus penalties

Use exact constraints for:

  • probability normalization;
  • nonnegativity;
  • the forward martingale condition;
  • hard static-arbitrage conditions.

Use penalties or bid-ask inequalities for noisy option observations.

12.4 Maturity consistency

Calibrating a separate terminal distribution at each maturity does not guarantee that the family is generated by a common martingale process. A dynamic regime model, martingale transport condition, or explicit inter-maturity consistency layer is required.

13. No-arbitrage validation

For European options with deterministic rates and dividends:

13.1 Put-call parity

C(K,T)−P(K,T)=S0e−qT−Ke−rT. C(K,T)-P(K,T) =S_0e^{-qT}-Ke^{-rT}. C(K,T)−P(K,T)=S0​e−qT−Ke−rT.

13.2 Bounds

max⁡(S0e−qT−Ke−rT,0)≤C(K,T)≤S0e−qT. \max(S_0e^{-qT}-Ke^{-rT},0) \le C(K,T)\le S_0e^{-qT}. max(S0​e−qT−Ke−rT,0)≤C(K,T)≤S0​e−qT.

13.3 Strike monotonicity

∂C∂K≤0. \frac{\partial C}{\partial K}\le0. ∂K∂C​≤0.

13.4 Strike convexity

∂2C∂K2≥0. \frac{\partial^2C}{\partial K^2}\ge0. ∂K2∂2C​≥0.

Under smoothness, the Breeden-Litzenberger identity gives

∂2C∂K2=D(0,T)fSTQ(K), \frac{\partial^2C}{\partial K^2} =D(0,T)f_{S_T}^Q(K), ∂K2∂2C​=D(0,T)fST​Q​(K),

linking option convexity to a nonnegative risk-neutral density [8]. For a discrete empirical law, the second derivative is a positive measure with atoms rather than an ordinary smooth density.

13.5 Forward martingale test

Numerically verify

∣∑iqiQST,i−F0,T∣<εF. \left| \sum_iq_i^QS_{T,i}-F_{0,T} \right|<\varepsilon_F. ∣∣​i∑​qiQ​ST,i​−F0,T​∣∣​<εF​.

13.6 Calendar consistency

Check calendar-spread constraints in an appropriate forward-normalized representation. Static strike arbitrage at every maturity does not by itself guarantee dynamic consistency across maturities.

14. Numerical and statistical validation

14.1 Cross-engine checks

Use direct finite-sum or high-accuracy deterministic convolution as the benchmark. Require

∣VFFT−Vbenchmark∣<εFFT, |V_{\mathrm{FFT}}-V_{\mathrm{benchmark}}|<\varepsilon_{\mathrm{FFT}}, ∣VFFT​−Vbenchmark​∣<εFFT​,

and

∣VMC−Vbenchmark∣≤z1−α/2SE⁡undefinedMC+εdisc. |V_{\mathrm{MC}}-V_{\mathrm{benchmark}}| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}_{MC} +\varepsilon_{\mathrm{disc}}. ∣VMC​−Vbenchmark​∣≤z1−α/2​SEMC​+εdisc​.

14.2 Scenario-count convergence

Test increasing NNN while holding the support policy fixed. Do not vary NNN and support simultaneously and then attribute all changes to discretization.

14.3 Support convergence

Vary tail probability cutoffs, endpoint nodes, and tail-completion methods separately.

14.4 Weight concentration

Effective scenario size:

NeffQ=1∑i(qiQ)2. N_{\mathrm{eff}}^Q =\frac{1}{\sum_i(q_i^Q)^2}. NeffQ​=∑i​(qiQ​)21​.

Entropy:

H(Q)=−∑iqiQlog⁡qiQ. H(Q)=-\sum_iq_i^Q\log q_i^Q. H(Q)=−i∑​qiQ​logqiQ​.

Maximum weight:

qmax⁡Q=max⁡iqiQ. q_{\max}^Q=\max_iq_i^Q. qmaxQ​=imax​qiQ​.

A very low NeffQN_{\mathrm{eff}}^QNeffQ​ indicates that pricing is controlled by very few scenarios.

14.5 Leave-one-extreme-out analysis

Recalculate prices and risk measures after removing:

  • the largest positive node;
  • the most negative node;
  • each major stress node;
  • each sparse historical crisis episode.

14.6 Rolling stability

Monitor through time:

PP,PQ,νk,λk,NeffQ,tail-node mass. P^P, \quad P^Q, \quad \nu_k, \quad \lambda_k, \quad N_{\mathrm{eff}}^Q, \quad \text{tail-node mass}. PP,PQ,νk​,λk​,NeffQ​,tail-node mass.

14.7 Out-of-sample trading validation

Evaluate:

  • predictive log score;
  • probability integral transform calibration;
  • left- and right-tail exceedance rates;
  • VaR conditional coverage;
  • ES backtests;
  • net P&L after costs;
  • turnover;
  • drawdown;
  • parameter stability.

15. Corrected conceptual points

15.1 LLN versus CLT

The law of large numbers concerns convergence of the sample mean to the population mean. The central limit theorem concerns the standardized sampling distribution of sums or means. Neither causes individual returns to become normal.

15.2 Symmetry versus reversal

A symmetric return density means equal centered left- and right-tail probabilities. It does not mean that a positive return must later be offset by a negative return of equal magnitude.

15.3 t30t_{30}t30​ versus Gaussian

t30t_{30}t30​ resembles a Gaussian over much of the body but retains polynomial tails. It therefore does not inherit the Gaussian MGF.

15.4 Empirical MGF versus population MGF

The empirical MGF is exact for the finite empirical law. It is not a regularization proof for the unbounded skew-ttt population.

15.5 Girsanov versus transforms

A change of measure specifies QQQ relative to PPP. An MGF or CGF is a transform used to characterize a chosen law and impose exponential-moment conditions. In Gaussian diffusion models, Girsanov and cumulant corrections are consistent pieces of the same risk-neutral construction, not interchangeable concepts.

15.6 Esscher tilt versus entropy projection

A log-return Esscher family uses the sufficient statistic xxx:

qi∝pieθxi. q_i\propto p_ie^{\theta x_i}. qi​∝pi​eθxi​.

A minimum-KL projection constrained on the gross return uses the sufficient statistic exe^xex:

qi∝pieβexi. q_i\propto p_i e^{\beta e^{x_i}}. qi​∝pi​eβexi​.

They are distinct unless the imposed feature is the same.

15.7 Regime-specific versus joint martingale constraints

Imposing mjQ(1)=ecm_j^Q(1)=e^cmjQ​(1)=ec in every state is sufficient but stronger than necessary. The correct condition for emissions attached to the arriving state is

PQmQ(1)=ec1. P^Q\mathbf m^Q(1)=e^c\mathbf1. PQmQ(1)=ec1.

15.8 Finite support and equivalence

Strictly positive PPP and QQQ weights on the same finite nodes give equivalent measures on that finite scenario space. This does not imply equivalence to a continuous unbounded skew-ttt law outside the chosen support.

16. Proposed production design

Layer 1: physical regime engine

Fit a standardized three-state skew-ttt HMM under PPP.

Layer 2: scenario engine

Construct deterministic quantile nodes, historical nodes, and governed stress nodes with documented probabilities.

Layer 3: empirical transform engine

Provide stable evaluations of

Mundefinedk(u),κundefinedk(u),ϕundefinedk(v), \widehat M_k(u), \quad \widehat\kappa_k(u), \quad \widehat\phi_k(v), Mk​(u),κk​(u),ϕ​k​(v),

using log-sum-exp and complex-safe arithmetic.

Layer 4: risk-neutral calibration

Offer at least three selectable methods:

  1. empirical log-return Esscher tilt;
  2. minimum-KL projection under forward and payoff constraints;
  3. full option-constrained entropy calibration.

Layer 5: horizon propagation

Use state-aware matrix transforms, deterministic convolution, or simulation based on product requirements.

Layer 6: pricing engines

Implement:

  1. direct finite-sum benchmark;
  2. deterministic grid convolution;
  3. adaptive Fourier quadrature;
  4. FFT or COS strip pricer;
  5. Monte Carlo;
  6. least-squares Monte Carlo for early exercise.

Layer 7: trading analytics

Produce physical regime probabilities, horizon return distributions, target probabilities, VaR, ES, expected payoff, and PPP-versus-QQQ divergence measures.

Layer 8: validation and governance

Automate martingale, parity, convexity, support, concentration, cross-engine, and rolling-stability checks.

17. Implementation pseudocode

17.1 Empirical CGF

function empirical_cgf(u, x, p):
    a_i = log(p_i) + u * x_i
    m = max(real-stabilizing component of a_i)
    return m + log(sum(exp(a_i - m)))

For complex uuu, use a real shift such as

m=max⁡iRe⁡(log⁡pi+uxi) m=\max_i\operatorname{Re}(\log p_i+ux_i) m=imax​Re(logpi​+uxi​)

so that the complex phase is retained.

17.2 Empirical Esscher calibration

function solve_esscher(carry, x, p):
    define g(theta):
        return cgf(theta + 1, x, p) - cgf(theta, x, p) - carry

    verify min(x) < carry < max(x)
    solve g(theta) = 0 by a bracketed root solver

    log_q_i = log(p_i) + theta * x_i
    normalize log_q with log-sum-exp
    return theta, q

17.3 Entropy projection

minimize sum_i q_i * log(q_i / p_i)
subject to:
    q_i >= 0
    sum_i q_i = 1
    sum_i q_i * exp(x_i) = forward_growth
    option bid <= sum_i q_i * discounted_payoff_i <= option ask

17.4 Regime transform propagation

for each transform argument u:
    D[u] = diag(mgf_state_1(u), ..., mgf_state_K(u))
    M_h[u] = alpha_Q_transpose * matrix_power(P_Q * D[u], h) * ones

The PQD(u)P^QD(u)PQD(u) ordering assumes arriving-state emissions.

18. Research extensions

  1. Time-varying transition probabilities driven by volatility, momentum, liquidity, and macro variables.
  2. State-dependent risk-neutral transition premia.
  3. Hierarchical shrinkage of λk\lambda_kλk​ toward zero and 1/νk1/\nu_k1/νk​ toward zero.
  4. Multivariate skew-ttt regimes with empirical copula or factor nodes.
  5. Martingale optimal transport between maturity-specific empirical marginals.
  6. Smooth entropy-regularized terminal densities rather than atomic laws.
  7. Joint calibration of returns, options, and variance swaps.
  8. Robust optimization over an ambiguity set around physical and risk-neutral scenario weights.
  9. Adjoint or automatic differentiation for calibration-aware Greeks.
  10. Regime-conditioned local or stochastic volatility overlays.

19. Final assessment

A mixed skew-ttt regime model can support coherent trading analytics and a derivative-pricing research platform if the physical and risk-neutral layers are kept conceptually separate.

The correct chain is

Skew-t regime model under P⟶governed finite scenario law⟶empirical transform⟶selected and calibrated Q⟶pricing and risk engines.

Skew-t regime model under P → governed finite scenario law → empirical transform → selected and calibrated Q → pricing and risk engines

The finite scenario law is the primitive pricing model. Its empirical MGF is computationally powerful because it is finite and exact for that law. Its use is legitimate provided the model documentation states that finiteness comes from finite support. The framework does not restore a nonexistent population MGF for an unbounded Student-ttt.

The most defensible production choice is an option-constrained minimum-relative-entropy calibration on a governed finite scenario grid, with the forward imposed exactly, liquid option constraints applied within bid-ask, transition and tail risk premia regularized, and all prices cross-checked by direct summation, Fourier methods, and Monte Carlo.

20. Version 2 design principles and model boundary

20.1 Primitive object and transform hierarchy

The primitive one-step object in regime kkk is the governed scenario law

LkP={(xk,i,pk,iP)}i=1Nk. \mathcal L_k^P=\{(x_{k,i},p_{k,i}^P)\}_{i=1}^{N_k}. LkP​={(xk,i​,pk,iP​)}i=1Nk​​.

The empirical MGF, CGF, and characteristic function are derived representations:

MundefinedkP(u)=∑ipk,iPeuxk,i,κundefinedkP(u)=log⁡MundefinedkP(u),ϕundefinedkP(v)=MundefinedkP(iv). \widehat M_k^P(u)=\sum_i p_{k,i}^P e^{ux_{k,i}},\qquad \widehat\kappa_k^P(u)=\log \widehat M_k^P(u),\qquad \widehat\phi_k^P(v)=\widehat M_k^P(iv). MkP​(u)=i∑​pk,iP​euxk,i​,κkP​(u)=logMkP​(u),ϕ​kP​(v)=MkP​(iv).

This hierarchy prevents an important category error. The framework is valid because it explicitly adopts a finite-state model. It is not valid because an empirical transform somehow regularizes the population transform of an unbounded skew-ttt law.

20.2 Three distinct probability objects

Production documentation and code must distinguish:

  1. Continuous physical reference law FkPF_k^PFkP​, used for estimation, interpretation, and generation of scenario candidates.
  2. Finite physical prior law FundefinedkP\widehat F_k^PFkP​, used as the governed scenario prior.
  3. Finite risk-neutral pricing law FundefinedkQ\widehat F_k^QFkQ​, obtained by a stated measure-selection and calibration procedure.

The map

FkP⟶FundefinedkP⟶FundefinedkQ F_k^P \longrightarrow \widehat F_k^P \longrightarrow \widehat F_k^Q FkP​⟶FkP​⟶FkQ​

contains two modelling interventions. The first is discretization and tail policy. The second is risk-neutralization. Their errors and sensitivities must be reported separately.

20.3 Interpretation of the calibrated model

When liquid options materially determine QQQ, the result should be described as an option-implied finite state-price law regularized toward a skew-ttt regime prior. It should not be presented as a pure skew-ttt option-pricing model. This wording correctly recognizes that the physical skew-ttt model may be only a prior once market option constraints are applied.

20.4 Intended scope

The architecture is most defensible for:

  • physical density and regime forecasting;
  • scenario-based risk measurement;
  • European and discretely monitored path-dependent pricing;
  • extraction of option-implied state prices;
  • controlled comparisons between physical and risk-neutral probabilities;
  • model-risk studies over alternative support and tail policies.

Additional modelling is required for deep-tail extrapolation, very long maturities, forward-skew products, continuously monitored barriers, American exercise under partial regime observation, and products whose value depends strongly on dynamics between calibrated maturities.

21. Statistical identification and physical calibration

21.1 Likelihood construction

Let x1:Tx_{1:T}x1:T​ denote observed log returns. For a KKK-state HMM with arriving-state emissions,

ℓ(ΘP)=∑t=1Tlog⁡[∑j=1Kαt∣t−1,jPfjP(xt;ϑjP)], \ell(\Theta^P)=\sum_{t=1}^T \log\left[ \sum_{j=1}^K \alpha_{t|t-1,j}^P f_j^P(x_t;\vartheta_j^P) \right], ℓ(ΘP)=t=1∑T​log[j=1∑K​αt∣t−1,jP​fjP​(xt​;ϑjP​)],

where

αt∣t−1,jP=∑i=1Kαt−1,iPpijP, \alpha_{t|t-1,j}^P=\sum_{i=1}^K \alpha_{t-1,i}^P p_{ij}^P, αt∣t−1,jP​=i=1∑K​αt−1,iP​pijP​,

and ϑjP=(μjP,σjP,νjP,λjP)\vartheta_j^P=(\mu_j^P,\sigma_j^P,\nu_j^P,\lambda_j^P)ϑjP​=(μjP​,σjP​,νjP​,λjP​). Evaluation must use scaled forward probabilities or log-domain recursions to avoid underflow.

21.2 Identification risks

Observed tail asymmetry can be explained by several substitutable mechanisms:

  • lower degrees of freedom νk\nu_kνk​;
  • larger scale σk\sigma_kσk​;
  • nonzero skew λk\lambda_kλk​;
  • greater stress-state occupancy;
  • more persistent stress transitions;
  • or an additional jump or stress node.

Consequently, unconstrained estimation can produce apparently excellent in-sample fit with unstable live state probabilities. A disciplined nested sequence is preferred:

  1. one-state Gaussian benchmark;
  2. Gaussian HMM;
  3. symmetric Student-ttt HMM;
  4. selectively skewed Student-ttt HMM;
  5. additional states only after out-of-sample evidence.

21.3 Penalized maximum likelihood

A representative physical objective is

min⁡ΘP−ℓ(ΘP)+λλ∑kλk2+λν∑k(log⁡νk−log⁡νˉ)2+λP∥PP−Pˉ∥F2. \min_{\Theta^P} -\ell(\Theta^P) +\lambda_\lambda\sum_k \lambda_k^2 +\lambda_\nu\sum_k \left(\log\nu_k-\log\bar\nu\right)^2 +\lambda_P\|P^P-\bar P\|_F^2. ΘPmin​−ℓ(ΘP)+λλ​k∑​λk2​+λν​k∑​(logνk​−logνˉ)2+λP​∥PP−Pˉ∥F2​.

The penalties shrink skewness toward symmetry, degrees of freedom toward a shared level, and transitions toward a stable reference matrix. Penalty strengths must be selected using rolling validation rather than in-sample likelihood alone.

21.4 Bayesian alternative

A Bayesian implementation may use:

  • logistic-normal or Dirichlet priors for rows of PPP^PPP;
  • ordered priors on σk\sigma_kσk​ to reduce label switching;
  • weakly informative priors on μk\mu_kμk​;
  • bounded transformed priors for λk\lambda_kλk​;
  • priors on νk−2\nu_k-2νk​−2 or νk−4\nu_k-4νk​−4, depending on required moments.

Posterior uncertainty should propagate into scenario weights and pricing-risk bands. A single maximum-likelihood estimate understates model uncertainty, particularly for rare regimes.

21.5 State ordering and label control

A stable labeling convention may impose

σ1<σ2<⋯<σK, \sigma_1<\sigma_2<\cdots<\sigma_K, σ1​<σ2​<⋯<σK​,

with secondary labels based on μk\mu_kμk​ or λk\lambda_kλk​. Ordering by volatility is operationally clearer than relabeling states after every calibration. If states overlap strongly, that is evidence that the selected KKK is too large.

21.6 Initialization and multi-start optimization

Recommended initialization:

  1. cluster returns using robust scale and sign-sensitive features;
  2. initialize μk\mu_kμk​ and σk\sigma_kσk​ from trimmed cluster statistics;
  3. initialize PPP^PPP with high diagonal persistence;
  4. start with common ν\nuν and λ=0\lambda=0λ=0;
  5. release parameters gradually;
  6. run multiple dispersed starts;
  7. retain solutions only if filtered-state paths and parameters are stable.

A best likelihood from a single start is not sufficient evidence of a valid optimum.

21.7 Physical calibration diagnostics

At minimum, report:

  • in-sample and rolling out-of-sample log scores;
  • probability integral transform histograms;
  • left- and right-tail exceedance rates;
  • regime occupancy and expected duration;
  • transition-count effective sample sizes;
  • parameter standard errors or posterior intervals;
  • filtered versus smoothed state paths;
  • likelihood-profile plots for νk\nu_kνk​ and λk\lambda_kλk​;
  • performance against simpler nested models.

The skew parameter should be retained only if it improves genuine predictive or economic criteria.

22. Scenario construction and tail completion

22.1 Probability-preserving quantization

Partition the continuous reference law into cells Ak,iA_{k,i}Ak,i​ and set

pk,iP=PP(X∈Ak,i∣S=k), p_{k,i}^P=P_P(X\in A_{k,i}\mid S=k), pk,iP​=PP​(X∈Ak,i​∣S=k),

with representative node

xk,i=EP[X∣X∈Ak,i,S=k] x_{k,i}=E_P[X\mid X\in A_{k,i},S=k] xk,i​=EP​[X∣X∈Ak,i​,S=k]

when this conditional mean is numerically available. This preserves cell mass and generally reduces weak-integration error relative to arbitrary point selection.

22.2 Moment and payoff-aware quantization

If the scenario grid is intended for option pricing, approximation quality should not be judged only by ordinary moments. It should also control errors in economically relevant features:

1,x,x2,ex,(S0ex−Km)+, 1,\quad x,\quad x^2,\quad e^x,\quad (S_0e^x-K_m)^+, 1,x,x2,ex,(S0​ex−Km​)+,

for representative strikes KmK_mKm​. A grid that approximates the return density well may still approximate convex payoffs poorly.

22.3 Hybrid body, tail, and stress grid

A robust grid may combine:

  • body quantile nodes from fitted skew-ttt regimes;
  • historical crisis observations;
  • option-implied right- and left-tail nodes;
  • governed stress nodes with separately documented probabilities.

Each node must carry metadata identifying its origin. This permits attribution of prices and risks to historical, parametric, option-implied, and judgmental components.

22.4 Repeated-stress problem

If a daily stress endpoint can recur independently at every step, a long-horizon path may contain several implausibly repeated crises. The model should therefore support one or more of:

  • a stress-arrival state with explicit intensity;
  • a semi-Markov duration model;
  • a cooldown state following a stress event;
  • non-repeatable event flags over a specified horizon;
  • horizon-specific terminal tail nodes;
  • state-dependent stress-node probabilities.

This is important whenever stress nodes are not ordinary recurrent daily returns.

22.5 Support policy report

Every calibration should store:

  • minimum and maximum node by regime and maturity;
  • tail probability represented by each endpoint cell;
  • whether the support is historical, truncated-parametric, spliced, or option-implied;
  • all added stress nodes and their rationale;
  • sensitivity under endpoint expansion and contraction;
  • contribution of endpoint nodes to EQ[eX]E_Q[e^X]EQ​[eX] and option prices.

23. Risk-neutral calibration in detail

23.1 Calibration hierarchy

Use the following hierarchy rather than jumping directly to an unrestricted option fit:

  1. verify support feasibility for the forward;
  2. obtain a forward-consistent baseline QQQ;
  3. fit liquid European options within bid-ask;
  4. regularize state and transition risk premia;
  5. enforce cross-strike no-arbitrage;
  6. enforce or test cross-maturity consistency;
  7. validate out of sample and under support perturbations.

23.2 Forward-only minimum-KL projection

Given prior weights pi>0p_i>0pi​>0, solve

min⁡q∑iqilog⁡qipi \min_q \sum_i q_i\log\frac{q_i}{p_i} qmin​i∑​qi​logpi​qi​​

subject to

∑iqi=1,∑iqiexi=ec. \sum_iq_i=1,\qquad \sum_iq_i e^{x_i}=e^c. i∑​qi​=1,i∑​qi​exi​=ec.

The dual is one-dimensional. With convention

qi(β)=pieβexiZ(β),Z(β)=∑jpjeβexj, q_i(\beta)=\frac{p_i e^{\beta e^{x_i}}}{Z(\beta)}, \qquad Z(\beta)=\sum_jp_j e^{\beta e^{x_j}}, qi​(β)=Z(β)pi​eβexi​​,Z(β)=j∑​pj​eβexj​,

the root equation is

h(β)=∑iqi(β)exi−ec=0. h(\beta)=\sum_i q_i(\beta)e^{x_i}-e^c=0. h(β)=i∑​qi​(β)exi​−ec=0.

Its derivative is

h′(β)=Var⁡q(β)(eX)≥0, h'(\beta)=\operatorname{Var}_{q(\beta)}(e^X)\ge0, h′(β)=Varq(β)​(eX)≥0,

and is strictly positive for nondegenerate gross-return nodes. Therefore an interior feasible target has a unique finite β\betaβ.

23.3 Multi-instrument entropy calibration

Let Gm,iG_{m,i}Gm,i​ be the discounted payoff of instrument mmm at node iii. With equality targets VmV_mVm​, solve

min⁡qDKL(q∥p) \min_q D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p) qmin​DKL​(q∥p)

subject to

Aq=b,q≥0. Aq=b,\qquad q\ge0. Aq=b,q≥0.

The dual parameterization is

$$
q_i(\boldsymbol\beta)

\frac{p_i\exp(\boldsymbol\beta^\top \mathbf g_i)}
{\sum_j p_j\exp(\boldsymbol\beta^\top \mathbf g_j)}.
$$

The dual Hessian is the covariance matrix of the feature vector under qqq:

∇2log⁡Z(β)=Cov⁡q(g). \nabla^2 \log Z(\boldsymbol\beta) =\operatorname{Cov}_q(\mathbf g). ∇2logZ(β)=Covq​(g).

Near linear dependence among payoff features creates ill-conditioning. Strike selection, feature scaling, and regularization are therefore essential.

Exact fit to every midpoint can overfit stale or inconsistent quotes. Prefer

Vmbid−ϵm−≤∑iqiGm,i≤Vmask+ϵm+, V_m^{\mathrm{bid}}-\epsilon_m^- \le \sum_iq_iG_{m,i} \le V_m^{\mathrm{ask}}+\epsilon_m^+, Vmbid​−ϵm−​≤i∑​qi​Gm,i​≤Vmask​+ϵm+​,

The forward, normalization, and nonnegativity constraints should remain exact unless data quality makes even the quoted forward unreliable.

23.5 Joint calibration of transitions and emissions

For a dynamic KKK-state model, variables may include

PQ,qk,iQ,α0Q. P^Q,\qquad q_{k,i}^Q,\qquad \alpha_0^Q. PQ,qk,iQ​,α0Q​.

A representative objective is

J=∑mwmρ ⁣(Vmmodel−Vmmidsm)+λq∑kDKL(qkQ∥pkP)+λP∑iDKL(pi⋅Q∥pi⋅P)+λTRT+λCRC, \begin{aligned} \mathcal J={}& \sum_m w_m \rho\!\left( \frac{V_m^{\mathrm{model}}-V_m^{\mathrm{mid}}}{s_m} \right) +\lambda_q\sum_kD_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_k^Q\|p_k^P)\\ &+\lambda_P\sum_iD_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_{i\cdot}^Q\|p_{i\cdot}^P) +\lambda_T\mathcal R_T +\lambda_C\mathcal R_C, \end{aligned} J=​m∑​wm​ρ(sm​Vmmodel​−Vmmid​​)+λq​k∑​DKL​(qkQ​∥pkP​)+λP​i∑​DKL​(pi⋅Q​∥pi⋅P​)+λT​RT​+λC​RC​,​
