and

PQmQ(1)=ec1. P^Q\mathbf m^Q(1)=e^c\mathbf1. PQmQ(1)=ec1.

23.6 Identifiability under QQQ

Vanilla options typically identify terminal state-price distributions more strongly than they identify a unique decomposition into transition and emission premia. Therefore:

  • do not freely calibrate all entries of PQP^QPQ and all node weights without shrinkage;
  • use economically interpretable low-dimensional transition tilts;
  • examine the profile objective along weakly identified directions;
  • report multiple near-optimal calibrations;
  • use exotic or forward-start information only when liquid enough to add identification.

23.7 Transition-matrix parameterizations

Useful parameterizations include:

Row-wise exponential tilt

pijQ=pijPexp⁡(ηij)∑ℓpiℓPexp⁡(ηiℓ). p_{ij}^Q= \frac{p_{ij}^P \exp(\eta_{ij})} {\sum_\ell p_{i\ell}^P\exp(\eta_{i\ell})}. pijQ​=∑ℓ​piℓP​exp(ηiℓ​)pijP​exp(ηij​)​.

Low-rank risk-premium tilt

ηij=ai+bj+zi⊤Rzj. \eta_{ij}=a_i+b_j+\mathbf z_i^\top R\mathbf z_j. ηij​=ai​+bj​+zi⊤​Rzj​.

Continuous-time generator

Estimate a valid generator GQG^QGQ and set

PQ(Δ)=exp⁡(ΔGQ). P^Q(\Delta)=\exp(\Delta G^Q). PQ(Δ)=exp(ΔGQ).

The generator approach gives time-step consistency but requires nonnegative off-diagonal intensities and zero row sums.

23.8 Calibration loss conventions

Possible quote losses include price error, implied-volatility error, and vega-scaled price error. Vega scaling is often useful:

εmvega=Vmmodel−Vmmarketmax⁡(Vegam,Vegamin⁡). \varepsilon_m^{\mathrm{vega}} =\frac{V_m^{\mathrm{model}}-V_m^{\mathrm{market}}} {\max(\mathrm{Vega}_m,\mathrm{Vega}_{\min})}. εmvega​=max(Vegam​,Vegamin​)Vmmodel​−Vmmarket​​.

However, deep options with poor liquidity should not gain excessive influence merely because of the scaling convention. Use liquidity weights, bid-ask widths, robust losses, and explicit quote filters.

23.9 Calibration algorithm

A stable sequence is:

  1. clean quotes and infer discount factors and forwards;
  2. enforce or project each market slice onto static-arbitrage constraints;
  3. build a support wide enough for all retained strikes;
  4. solve the forward-only entropy projection;
  5. add option constraints from liquid to less liquid strikes;
  6. calibrate low-dimensional transition premia;
  7. expand degrees of freedom only if validation improves;
  8. calculate exact constraint residuals;
  9. perturb quotes, support, priors, and starting values;
  10. retain calibration ensembles when non-uniqueness is material.

23.10 Posterior-prior displacement diagnostics

Report:

DKL(Q∥P),DKL(P∥Q),12∑i∣qi−pi∣, D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P),\quad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q),\quad \frac12\sum_i|q_i-p_i|, DKL​(Q∥P),DKL​(P∥Q),21​i∑​∣qi​−pi​∣,

as well as Wasserstein distance, maximum likelihood ratio max⁡i(qi/pi)\max_i(q_i/p_i)maxi​(qi​/pi​), minimum likelihood ratio, tail-mass migration, and effective scenario count. These reveal whether the physical skew-ttt prior still materially influences the calibrated pricing law.

24. Maturity consistency and dynamic completion

24.1 Marginal versus dynamic calibration

A separate terminal law QTQ_TQT​ for each maturity may price European options correctly while failing to define a common process. Dynamic products require transition kernels KTa,TbK_{T_a,T_b}KTa​,Tb​​ satisfying

qTb(y)=∑xqTa(x)KTa,Tb(x,y) q_{T_b}(y)=\sum_x q_{T_a}(x)K_{T_a,T_b}(x,y) qTb​​(y)=x∑​qTa​​(x)KTa​,Tb​​(x,y)

and the martingale restriction

∑yKTa,Tb(x,y)S(y)=S(x)eca,b. \sum_y K_{T_a,T_b}(x,y)S(y) =S(x)e^{c_{a,b}}. y∑​KTa​,Tb​​(x,y)S(y)=S(x)eca,b​.

24.2 Dynamic completion alternatives

Possible approaches are:

  • calibrate one common regime process jointly to all maturities;
  • construct martingale transport couplings between calibrated marginals;
  • fit maturity-dependent but smoothly varying transition matrices;
  • use an entropy-minimizing path measure subject to all option constraints;
  • use a Markov-chain projection that matches marginal state prices.

24.3 Calendar-arbitrage checks

For deterministic discounting, call prices expressed as functions of forward moneyness should satisfy suitable calendar monotonicity conditions. At a minimum:

  • total implied variance should not create calendar-spread arbitrage;
  • later marginal laws must be reachable from earlier laws under a martingale coupling;
  • interpolated maturities must preserve convexity and forward consistency.

24.4 Path-space entropy calibration

Let ω\omegaω denote a complete regime and return-node path with physical prior probability P(ω)P(\omega)P(ω). A dynamic minimum-entropy model solves

min⁡Q∑ωQ(ω)log⁡Q(ω)P(ω) \min_Q \sum_\omega Q(\omega) \log\frac{Q(\omega)}{P(\omega)} Qmin​ω∑​Q(ω)logP(ω)Q(ω)​

subject to normalization, conditional martingale restrictions, and option-price constraints across maturities. This is conceptually clean but computationally large. Dynamic programming, factorized likelihood ratios, iterative proportional fitting, or stochastic optimization may be required.

25. Analytical and semi-analytical pricing

25.1 Exact finite-sum formula

For terminal nodes (xi,qi)(x_i,q_i)(xi​,qi​) and payoff Π\PiΠ,

V0=D(0,T)∑iqiΠ(S0exi). V_0=D(0,T)\sum_iq_i\Pi(S_0e^{x_i}). V0​=D(0,T)i∑​qi​Π(S0​exi​).

This is the primary analytical formula under a terminal finite law. For European calls,

C0=D(0,T)∑iqi(S0exi−K)+. C_0=D(0,T)\sum_iq_i(S_0e^{x_i}-K)^+. C0​=D(0,T)i∑​qi​(S0​exi​−K)+.

For a discrete law, a strip of strikes can be priced efficiently after sorting terminal prices and precomputing right-tail sums:

Aj=∑i≥jqiSi,Bj=∑i≥jqi. A_j=\sum_{i\ge j}q_iS_i,\qquad B_j=\sum_{i\ge j}q_i. Aj​=i≥j∑​qi​Si​,Bj​=i≥j∑​qi​.

Then for a strike between nodes Sj−1<K≤SjS_{j-1}<K\le S_jSj−1​<K≤Sj​,

C(K)=D(0,T)(Aj−KBj). C(K)=D(0,T)(A_j-KB_j). C(K)=D(0,T)(Aj​−KBj​).

This gives near-constant-time evaluation per strike after sorting.

25.2 Matrix-transform formula

For homogeneous transitions and arriving-state emissions,

MhQ(u)=α0Q⊤[PQDQ(u)]h1. M_h^Q(u)=\alpha_0^{Q\top} [P^QD^Q(u)]^h\mathbf1. MhQ​(u)=α0Q⊤​[PQDQ(u)]h1.

For time-varying dynamics,

M0,hQ(u)=α0Q⊤∏n=1h[PnQDnQ(u)]1, M_{0,h}^Q(u)= \alpha_0^{Q\top} \prod_{n=1}^h[P_n^QD_n^Q(u)]\mathbf1, M0,hQ​(u)=α0Q⊤​n=1∏h​[PnQ​DnQ​(u)]1,

with chronological matrix ordering fixed explicitly.

25.3 Closed forms under special emission choices

True closed forms may exist if regime-conditional dynamics are Gaussian, affine, phase-type, or otherwise transform-tractable. The general empirical atomic model does not require a continuous-density closed form because direct summation is already exact. Analytical approximations are mainly useful for:

  • controls in Monte Carlo;
  • initial guesses in calibration;
  • sanity checks;
  • fast approximations when the terminal support is extremely large.

25.4 Moment-matched approximations

A Gaussian, shifted-lognormal, or saddlepoint approximation can be fitted to selected cumulants of the finite law. Such approximations must not replace the exact finite-sum benchmark without documented error. Saddlepoint formulas also require care near support boundaries and payoff discontinuities.

26. Deterministic quadrature

26.1 When quadrature is appropriate

For the unsmoothed atomic law, quadrature is unnecessary because the expectation is a finite sum. Quadrature becomes useful when:

  • continuous skew-ttt bodies are truncated and retained;
  • smooth tail completion is attached;
  • kernel smoothing replaces each atom by a local density;
  • a conditional continuous factor remains after discrete regime conditioning;
  • calibration integrates over latent variables.

26.2 Domain decomposition

For a European call, split at

xK=log⁡(K/S0). x_K=\log(K/S_0). xK​=log(K/S0​).

Then

C0=D(0,T)∫xKU(S0ex−K)fTQ(x) dx, C_0=D(0,T)\int_{x_K}^{U}(S_0e^x-K)f_T^Q(x)\,dx, C0​=D(0,T)∫xK​U​(S0​ex−K)fTQ​(x)dx,

plus any explicit tail contribution beyond UUU. Splitting at payoff kinks prevents an adaptive integrator from wasting evaluations around nonsmooth points.

26.3 Recommended rules

  • Gauss-Kronrod: general one-dimensional adaptive benchmark.
  • Gauss-Legendre: efficient after mapping to a finite interval.
  • Clenshaw-Curtis: useful for nested grids and repeated evaluations.
  • Double-exponential or tanh-sinh: useful near endpoint singularities or difficult transformed tails.
  • Gauss-Hermite: useful for conditionally Gaussian factors, not as a default rule for skew-ttt tails.
  • Sparse grids: possible for a small number of continuous factors, but dimensionality grows rapidly.

26.4 Error controls

Separate:

$$
\text{total error}
= ext{tail truncation error}

  • ext{quadrature error}
  • ext{interpolation error}
  • ext{model error}.
    $$

Run absolute and relative tolerance tests, interval expansion tests, and independent comparison with a high-order or arbitrary-precision benchmark for selected cases.

27. Fourier quadrature, FFT, and COS methods

27.1 Characteristic function

For a terminal finite law,

ϕT(v)=∑iqieivxi. \phi_T(v)=\sum_iq_i e^{ivx_i}. ϕT​(v)=i∑​qi​eivxi​.

For regime dynamics it follows from the matrix product. Complex arguments required by damped pricing must be evaluated using real-part stabilization.

27.2 Direct Fourier quadrature

For isolated strikes, direct adaptive integration in Fourier space is often preferable to FFT. It avoids grid-induced strike interpolation and allows local control of oscillatory error. The implementation must specify:

  • transform convention;
  • damping or contour shift;
  • integration cutoff;
  • oscillatory quadrature rule;
  • handling near zero frequency;
  • branch conventions for complex logarithms.

27.3 Carr-Madan FFT

For log strike kkk, apply damping

Cundefined(k)=eαkC(k),α>0, \widetilde C(k)=e^{\alpha k}C(k),\qquad \alpha>0, C(k)=eαkC(k),α>0,

and use the shifted characteristic function. Under finite support all exponential moments exist, but large α\alphaα can still cause severe scaling and cancellation. Numerical admissibility is not the same as mathematical existence.

A practical FFT implementation must manage:

  • frequency spacing η\etaη;
  • number of points NNN;
  • log-strike spacing λ=2π/(Nη)\lambda=2\pi/(N\eta)λ=2π/(Nη);
  • strike range;
  • Simpson or higher-order weights;
  • phase shifts;
  • aliasing;
  • interpolation back to quoted strikes.

27.4 COS method

The COS method expands the density or payoff over a finite interval [a,b][a,b][a,b]. It can be highly efficient for smooth distributions with well-controlled truncation. For an atomic law, the characteristic function is easy to evaluate, but Gibbs-type behavior and nonsmooth Greeks can arise because the terminal measure contains atoms. Smoothing or direct summation may therefore be superior unless multi-step propagation has produced a sufficiently regular grid law.

27.5 Fourier-space time stepping

For Bermudan, barrier, and regime-switching problems, one may alternate:

  1. transform the state-conditioned value function;
  2. multiply by the one-step transition-emission symbol;
  3. invert the transform;
  4. apply barriers or early-exercise conditions;
  5. repeat backward in time.

This is attractive when transition is convolutional in log price. Care is required around barriers, absorbing states, wraparound, and discontinuous exercise boundaries.

27.6 Fourier validation

Require convergence under simultaneous changes in:

  • NNN;
  • frequency spacing;
  • damping;
  • log-strike domain;
  • truncation interval;
  • interpolation scheme.

A single apparently stable FFT price is not evidence of convergence. Compare each test case against direct summation or deterministic convolution.

28. Monte Carlo and quasi-Monte Carlo

28.1 Exact simulation of the finite model

No Euler discretization is required for the one-step finite scenario process. Given state St=iS_t=iSt​=i:

  1. sample arriving state St+1=jS_{t+1}=jSt+1​=j from row iii of PQP^QPQ;
  2. sample return node xj,nx_{j,n}xj,n​ from qj,nQq_{j,n}^Qqj,nQ​;
  3. update St+1asset=Stassetexj,nS_{t+1}^{\mathrm{asset}}=S_t^{\mathrm{asset}}e^{x_{j,n}}St+1asset​=Stasset​exj,n​;
  4. update path statistics and continue.

The only time discretization is the model’s own step size.

28.2 Variance reduction

Useful methods include:

  • analytical or direct-sum European control variates;
  • stratification by current state or terminal state;
  • stratification by number of stress-state visits;
  • conditional Monte Carlo over return nodes given the regime path;
  • common random numbers across calibration candidates;
  • randomized quasi-Monte Carlo for inverse-CDF draws;
  • importance sampling toward barrier or tail events.

Antithetic sampling is not automatically effective for asymmetric discrete laws and should be validated rather than assumed.

28.3 Conditional Monte Carlo

If the regime path is simulated but emission aggregation can be convolved exactly conditional on that path, integrate over emissions rather than sampling them. Conversely, if the number of regime paths is manageable, sum over regime paths and simulate only continuous overlays. Rao-Blackwellization can materially reduce variance.

28.4 Rare-event importance sampling

For a rare event AAA, simulate under proposal Qundefined\widetilde QQ​ and use

V0=D(0,T)EQundefined[ΠdQdQundefined]. V_0=D(0,T)E_{\widetilde Q} \left[ \Pi\frac{dQ}{d\widetilde Q} \right]. V0​=D(0,T)EQ​​[ΠdQ​dQ​].

In a finite state-path model, the likelihood ratio is the product of transition and emission probability ratios. Proposal probabilities must remain positive wherever the original model assigns positive probability to a payoff-relevant path.

28.5 Greeks

Methods include:

  • bump-and-revalue with common random numbers;
  • likelihood-ratio estimators for probability parameters;
  • pathwise derivatives when payoff and parameterization are smooth;
  • algorithmic differentiation through calibration and simulation;
  • conditional smoothing around payoff kinks.

For atomic laws, naive pathwise gamma is unreliable because exercise indicators jump at node crossings.

28.6 Monte Carlo stopping rule

Report the discounted standard error

SEundefined=D(0,T)sΠM, \widehat{\mathrm{SE}}= D(0,T)\frac{s_\Pi}{\sqrt M}, SE=D(0,T)M​sΠ​​,

confidence intervals, effective sample size under importance sampling, and replication-to-replication stability. Stop only when both statistical error and implementation bias are below product-specific tolerances.

29. Trees, lattices, and dynamic programming

29.1 Nonrecombining scenario tree

A literal tree branches by arriving regime and return node. Its node count grows exponentially. It is exact for short horizons but quickly becomes infeasible.

29.2 Recombining log-price lattice

Map log prices onto grid points ym=y0+mΔyy_m=y_0+m\Delta yym​=y0​+mΔy. After each transition, distribute probability to neighboring grid points while preserving, where possible:

∑mwm=1,∑mwmeym=target gross first moment. \sum_m w_m=1, \qquad \sum_mw_m e^{y_m}=\text{target gross first moment}. m∑​wm​=1,m∑​wm​eym​=target gross first moment.

Moment-preserving interpolation is preferable to nearest-grid projection. Record mass and martingale residuals after every step.

29.3 State-conditioned Bellman recursion

For regime-observable value Vn(s,k)V_n(s,k)Vn​(s,k),

Vn(s,k)=Dn∑jpkjQ∑iqj,iQVn+1(sexj,i,j). V_n(s,k)=D_n \sum_jp_{kj}^Q \sum_iq_{j,i}^Q V_{n+1}(se^{x_{j,i}},j). Vn​(s,k)=Dn​j∑​pkjQ​i∑​qj,iQ​Vn+1​(sexj,i​,j).

For a Bermudan option,

Vn(s,k)=max⁡{Πn(s),  Dn∑jpkjQ∑iqj,iQVn+1(sexj,i,j)}. V_n(s,k)=\max\left\{ \Pi_n(s),\; D_n\sum_jp_{kj}^Q\sum_iq_{j,i}^QV_{n+1}(se^{x_{j,i}},j) \right\}. Vn​(s,k)=max{Πn​(s),Dn​j∑​pkjQ​i∑​qj,iQ​Vn+1​(sexj,i​,j)}.

29.4 Partial observation

If the regime is unobservable, the sufficient state is generally the belief vector

αt=(P(St=1∣Ft),…,P(St=K∣Ft)). \boldsymbol\alpha_t=(P(S_t=1\mid\mathcal F_t),\ldots,P(S_t=K\mid\mathcal F_t)). αt​=(P(St​=1∣Ft​),…,P(St​=K∣Ft​)).

An exact tree in (s,α)(s,\boldsymbol\alpha)(s,α) is high-dimensional. Approaches include belief-grid interpolation, particle filtering inside simulation, regression Monte Carlo, and approximations that freeze or compress the belief state. Pricing as if the latent state were directly observable can materially overstate the information available to the exercise policy.

29.5 Tree validation

Check:

  • probability conservation;
  • one-step and multi-step martingale residuals;
  • convergence under Δy\Delta yΔy and Δt\Delta tΔt refinement;
  • sensitivity to interpolation;
  • agreement with direct sums for European claims;
  • monotonicity and convexity in strike;
  • stability of early-exercise boundaries.

30. Finite difference, PIDE, and Fourier-space time stepping

30.1 Important model distinction

A pure finite-scenario discrete-time process does not naturally generate a classical local diffusion PDE. Its backward equation is an expectation recursion. A finite-difference PDE becomes appropriate only after embedding or approximating the model by a continuous-time diffusion, jump process, or Markov-chain generator.

30.2 Continuous-time regime-switching generator

Suppose regime kkk has local diffusion coefficients μkQ\mu_k^QμkQ​ and σk\sigma_kσk​ and generator GQ=(gkℓQ)G^Q=(g_{k\ell}^Q)GQ=(gkℓQ​). Then a European value vector Vk(t,s)V_k(t,s)Vk​(t,s) satisfies a coupled system of the form

∂Vk∂t+(r−q)s∂Vk∂s+12σk2s2∂2Vk∂s2−rVk+∑ℓ≠kgkℓQ(Vℓ−Vk)=0. \frac{\partial V_k}{\partial t} +(r-q)s\frac{\partial V_k}{\partial s} +\frac12\sigma_k^2s^2\frac{\partial^2V_k}{\partial s^2} -rV_k +\sum_{\ell\ne k}g_{k\ell}^Q(V_\ell-V_k)=0. ∂t∂Vk​​+(r−q)s∂s∂Vk​​+21​σk2​s2∂s2∂2Vk​​−rVk​+ℓ=k∑​gkℓQ​(Vℓ​−Vk​)=0.

If jumps or a continuous tail-completion component are included, add the compensated integral operator, producing a PIDE.

30.3 Discrete scenario jump operator

For a continuous-time finite jump measure with intensities λk,i\lambda_{k,i}λk,i​ and log jumps xk,ix_{k,i}xk,i​, the jump term is

JkV(s)=∑iλk,i[V(sexk,i)−V(s)−s(exk,i−1)Vs(s)], \mathcal J_kV(s) =\sum_i\lambda_{k,i} \left[ V(se^{x_{k,i}})-V(s)-s(e^{x_{k,i}}-1)V_s(s) \right], Jk​V(s)=i∑​λk,i​[V(sexk,i​)−V(s)−s(exk,i​−1)Vs​(s)],

subject to the chosen truncation convention. Because the jump support is finite, the integral operator becomes a weighted sum but still requires interpolation at off-grid values sexk,ise^{x_{k,i}}sexk,i​.

30.4 Schemes

Recommended schemes include:

  • fully implicit Euler for robustness;
  • Crank-Nicolson with initial damping steps for nonsmooth payoffs;
  • IMEX schemes treating local diffusion implicitly and jump terms explicitly or semi-implicitly;
  • operator splitting between diffusion, jumps, and regime coupling;
  • penalty or policy-iteration methods for American exercise;
  • monotone schemes where preservation of no-arbitrage properties is critical.

30.5 Stability and positivity

The numerical operator should preserve, as far as possible:

  • nonnegative option values;
  • monotonicity in spot;
  • convexity for vanilla payoffs;
  • appropriate boundary behavior;
  • stable regime coupling.

Central differencing can create oscillations when drift dominates. Upwinding, flux limiting, or transformed coordinates may be necessary.

30.6 Boundary conditions

For a call on a non-dividend-paying asset, typical asymptotic boundaries are

V(t,0)=0, V(t,0)=0, V(t,0)=0,

and at large Smax⁡S_{\max}Smax​,

V(t,Smax⁡)≈Smax⁡−KD(t,T), V(t,S_{\max})\approx S_{\max}-K D(t,T), V(t,Smax​)≈Smax​−KD(t,T),

adjusted for dividends and product features. Barrier and rebate contracts require contract-specific boundary conditions. Boundary truncation must be tested separately from spatial and temporal discretization.

30.7 American complementarity problem

For each regime,

max⁡(LQV−rV+Vt,  Π−V)=0, \max\left( \mathcal L^Q V-rV+V_t,\; \Pi-V \right)=0, max(LQV−rV+Vt​,Π−V)=0,

with coupling between regimes. Penalty methods, projected iterative solvers, or policy iteration can solve the resulting discrete linear-complementarity system.

30.8 When FD or PIDE is worth using

FD/PIDE methods are attractive for:

  • American and Bermudan claims;
  • barriers and rebates;
  • state-dependent boundaries;
  • models with local diffusion overlays;
  • products naturally expressed by backward state-space recursion.

They are usually unnecessary for a one-maturity European payoff under a modest atomic terminal law, where direct summation is exact and simpler.

31. Engine-selection matrix

Use the following practical hierarchy:

  • European, modest terminal support: direct finite sum.
  • Many strikes, large propagated support: sorted tail sums, FFT, or COS after validation.
  • One or a few strikes with smooth continuous completion: adaptive quadrature or direct Fourier quadrature.
  • Path-dependent, high-dimensional, or exposure simulation: Monte Carlo or quasi-Monte Carlo.
  • Bermudan or American with manageable state dimension: lattice, dynamic programming, FD, or LSMC.
  • Barriers with convolutional transitions: lattice, Fourier-space time stepping, FD/PIDE, or Brownian/jump bridge-adjusted MC where applicable.
  • Partial observation: simulation or belief-state dynamic programming.
  • Calibration loop: use the fastest engine that remains exact or tightly controlled for the quote set, with slower engines as independent validators.

No single engine should be declared universally best. Product structure, state dimension, monitoring convention, calibration frequency, and required Greeks determine the choice.

32. Software architecture and implementation specification

32.1 Core modules

A production library should separate:

  1. physical_model: skew-ttt density, HMM filtering, estimation, diagnostics.
  2. scenario_builder: quantization, historical nodes, stress nodes, tail completion.
  3. transform_engine: MGF, CGF, CF, matrix products, stabilization.
  4. risk_neutral_calibrator: Esscher, entropy, bid-ask, transition calibration.
  5. distribution_propagator: convolution, lattice, transform, and path simulation.
  6. pricing_engines: direct sum, quadrature, Fourier, FFT, COS, MC, tree, FD/PIDE.
  7. greeks_engine: fixed-law, recalibrated, and adjoint sensitivities.
  8. validation: martingale, arbitrage, convergence, support, and concentration tests.
  9. market_data: curves, forwards, dividends, corporate actions, quote cleaning.
  10. audit_store: inputs, parameters, solver traces, seeds, tolerances, and hashes.

32.2 Canonical data structures

A scenario law should store:

ScenarioLaw
    nodes_log_return[N]
    probabilities[N]
    regime_id
    horizon
    measure_tag            # P-prior or Q-pricing
    source_tag[N]          # historical, quantile, stress, implied
    support_policy
    tail_metadata
    calibration_id

A dynamic model should store transition conventions explicitly:

RegimeModel
    transition_matrix[K,K]
    emission_laws[K]
    emission_timing        # arriving-state or departing-state
    time_step
    initial_state_prob[K]
    rate_curve_id
    dividend_curve_id

32.3 Numerical safeguards

Mandatory safeguards include:

  • log-sum-exp normalization;
  • scaled HMM forward recursion;
  • bracketed scalar root solvers;
  • constrained convex solvers for entropy calibration;
  • row-stochasticity projections only with audit logging;
  • deterministic random seeds for regression tests;
  • explicit complex transform conventions;
  • checks for NaN, infinity, negative probabilities, and lost mass;
  • compensated or pairwise summation where weight scales are extreme.

32.4 Pseudocode for robust entropy calibration

function calibrate_entropy(prior_p, features_G, targets_or_bounds):
    validate prior_p > 0 and sum(prior_p) = 1
    scale each feature column
    test convex-hull feasibility or solve a feasibility program
    initialize dual variables at zero
    solve convex dual using damped Newton or trust region
    recover q in log space
    verify q >= 0 and sum(q) = 1
    verify forward residual at strict tolerance
    verify option residuals or bid-ask inclusion
    compute Hessian condition number and displacement diagnostics
    return q, dual_variables, diagnostics

32.5 Pseudocode for exact regime simulation

function simulate_path(model_Q, spot0, steps, rng):
    state = draw(model_Q.initial_state_prob, rng)
    spot = spot0
    path = [spot]
    for n in 1..steps:
        next_state = draw(model_Q.P_Q[state, :], rng)
        x = draw(model_Q.emission_law_Q[next_state], rng)
        spot = spot * exp(x)
        state = next_state
        append(path, spot)
    return path

32.6 Reproducibility

Every result must retain:

  • source-data timestamp and checksum;
  • code version and build identifier;
  • model configuration;
  • optimizer, tolerances, and stopping reason;
  • random-number generator and seed;
  • support and tail policy;
  • excluded quotes and reasons;
  • calibration residuals;
  • validation results;
  • hardware and precision where numerically material.

33. Greeks, hedging, and calibration risk

33.1 Three Greek definitions

Distinguish:

  1. Frozen-law Greek: nodes and QQQ weights fixed.
  2. Market-rule Greek: curves, forward, and smile moved according to a stated sticky convention.
  3. Recalibrated Greek: the complete model is recalibrated after the market bump.

These can differ materially. A risk report must identify which definition is used.

33.2 Implicit differentiation through calibration

If calibrated parameters θ∗(z)\theta^*(z)θ∗(z) solve

F(θ,z)=0, F(\theta,z)=0, F(θ,z)=0,

then, when regularity holds,

dθ∗dz=−(∂F∂θ)−1∂F∂z. \frac{d\theta^*}{dz} =-\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial\theta}\right)^{-1} \frac{\partial F}{\partial z}. dzdθ∗​=−(∂θ∂F​)−1∂z∂F​.

For value V(θ∗(z),z)V(\theta^*(z),z)V(θ∗(z),z),

dVdz=Vz+Vθdθ∗dz. \frac{dV}{dz} =V_z+V_\theta\frac{d\theta^*}{dz}. dzdV​=Vz​+Vθ​dzdθ∗​.

This is preferable to noisy repeated optimization when the active constraint set is stable. Bid-ask inequalities and changing active sets can create nonsmooth sensitivities.

33.3 Model-risk Greeks

In addition to market Greeks, calculate sensitivity to:

  • support endpoints;
  • stress-node probabilities;
  • KL regularization strength;
  • transition-risk-premium penalty;
  • number of regimes;
  • degrees-of-freedom constraints;
  • maturity-coupling strength;
  • smoothing bandwidth.

These are not hedge ratios, but they quantify valuation uncertainty caused by modelling choices.

34. Validation, benchmarking, and acceptance criteria

34.1 Model benchmarks

Compare against:

  • Black-Scholes or Bachelier where appropriate;
  • Gaussian mixture;
  • symmetric Student-ttt regime model;
  • two-state versus three-state HMM;
  • direct option-implied discrete density without a skew-ttt prior;
  • a standard stochastic-volatility or exponential-Lévy benchmark where relevant.

Complexity is justified only if it improves out-of-sample performance, stability, or product coverage.

34.2 Synthetic recovery tests

Generate data from known parameter sets and verify:

  • parameter recovery under adequate samples;
  • regime classification accuracy;
  • transition recovery;
  • calibration recovery from synthetic option prices;
  • robustness when the fitted model is misspecified;
  • confidence-interval coverage.

34.3 Engine unit tests

Include cases with:

  • one node, where results are deterministic;
  • two nodes with hand-calculable prices;
  • one regime reducing to an ordinary finite law;
  • identical regime emissions, making transitions irrelevant to terminal returns;
  • zero rates and dividends;
  • strikes below all nodes and above all nodes;
  • limiting probabilities approaching zero;
  • boundary forward feasibility.

34.4 Cross-engine acceptance

For a benchmark price V∗V_*V∗​:

∣Vquad−V∗∣≤εquad, |V_{\mathrm{quad}}-V_*|\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{quad}}, ∣Vquad​−V∗​∣≤εquad​,

∣VFFT−V∗∣≤εFFT, |V_{\mathrm{FFT}}-V_*|\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{FFT}}, ∣VFFT​−V∗​∣≤εFFT​,

and

∣VMC−V∗∣≤z1−α/2SEundefinedMC+εbias. |V_{\mathrm{MC}}-V_*| \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_{MC} +\varepsilon_{\mathrm{bias}}. ∣VMC​−V∗​∣≤z1−α/2​SEMC​+εbias​.

FD and lattice errors should exhibit the expected refinement behavior until interpolation, boundary, or payoff nonsmoothness dominates.

34.5 Calibration acceptance

A calibration is accepted only if:

  • normalization and nonnegativity pass strict tolerances;
  • the forward martingale residual passes;
  • retained liquid options lie within bid-ask or approved tolerances;
  • strike monotonicity and convexity pass;
  • calendar checks pass;
  • weight concentration remains within limits;
  • support perturbations do not cause unacceptable price changes;
  • multiple starts reach economically consistent solutions;
  • calibration displacement from the prior is explainable.

34.6 Challenger and fallback

Production governance should define:

  • a simpler challenger model;
  • conditions triggering fallback;
  • stale-market procedures;
  • maximum permitted calibration displacement;
  • support-extension rules;
  • limits on stress-node contribution;
  • manual override and approval requirements.

35. Revised implementation roadmap

Phase 1: deterministic one-period prototype

Implement scenario laws, stable transforms, direct pricing, Esscher calibration, forward-only entropy projection, and exact unit tests.

Phase 2: physical HMM

Implement Gaussian and symmetric-ttt benchmarks before selective skew-ttt regimes. Add rolling filtering, forecast scoring, and parameter-stability diagnostics.

Phase 3: option-constrained terminal calibration

Add quote cleaning, bid-ask entropy calibration, static-arbitrage checks, tail-node governance, and posterior-prior displacement reports.

Phase 4: multi-step dynamics

Implement regime-aware convolution and exact Monte Carlo. Validate all European claims against deterministic propagation.

Phase 5: Fourier engines

Add direct Fourier quadrature, FFT, and COS only after transform conventions and direct benchmarks are stable.

Phase 6: early exercise and barriers

Add recombining lattice or grid dynamic programming, then FD/PIDE or Fourier-space time stepping where a continuous-time embedding is justified. Add LSMC for higher-dimensional path dependence.

Phase 7: maturity consistency

Jointly calibrate a dynamic model or construct martingale couplings between maturity slices. Do not claim dynamic exotic capability before this layer passes validation.

Phase 8: production controls

Add calibration ensembles, audit persistence, performance engineering, parallel pricing, automatic differentiation, monitoring dashboards, and independent model validation.

36. Revised final assessment

The framework is best understood as a governed finite-state pricing and risk architecture with a skew-ttt regime model supplying physical structure and prior information. The empirical MGF is an exact and useful transform of the finite law, but it is not the source of economic legitimacy and does not restore the missing population MGF of an unbounded Student-ttt law.

The most defensible chain is

continuous skew-t HMM under P→governed finite P prior→martingale- and option-constrained finite Q→dynamically consistent propagation→product-specific pricing engine. \boxed{ \text{continuous skew-}t\text{ HMM under }P \rightarrow \text{governed finite }P\text{ prior} \rightarrow \text{martingale- and option-constrained finite }Q \rightarrow \text{dynamically consistent propagation} \rightarrow \text{product-specific pricing engine} }. continuous skew-t HMM under P→governed finite P prior→martingale- and option-constrained finite Q→dynamically consistent propagation→product-specific pricing engine​.

The preferred European calibration is an option-constrained minimum-relative-entropy projection with exact forward consistency, bid-ask treatment of quotes, explicit support and tail governance, and quantified displacement from the physical prior. For dynamic and path-dependent products, separately calibrated terminal laws are insufficient. A common risk-neutral process or a valid sequence of martingale transition kernels is required.

Direct finite summation should remain the principal benchmark. Quadrature is appropriate for continuous completion; Fourier quadrature, FFT, and COS are scale tools; Monte Carlo is the flexible path-dependent engine; trees and lattices support transparent dynamic programming; and FD/PIDE methods are justified only after a continuous-time diffusion or jump embedding has been specified. Engine choice must follow the product and model structure rather than fashion.

The decisive empirical question is whether this architecture improves out-of-sample density forecasts, option fits, stability, or product coverage relative to simpler models after complexity and model risk are penalized. If it does not, the simpler challenger should be preferred. If it does, the framework can serve as a coherent bridge between physical heavy-tail regime analysis, option-implied state prices, and controlled derivative-pricing computation.
